articles.title: Russian attacks kill 7, injure dozens across Ukraine amid continued strikes on energy infrastructure
articles.body:
Russia launches 'one of its largest attacks' on Ukraine's energy grid as US 'disregards' Graham's sanctions, Zelensky says
Editor's note: The story has been updated to include comments from President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Russian attacks against Ukraine killed seven people and injured around 90 over the past day, regional authorities said on Oct. 17, with the country reporting one of the heaviest Russian attacks against energy infrastructure so far.
Ukrainian forces downed 289 out of the 332 drones, including jet-powered attack drones, launched by Russia overnight, the Air Force reported. Russian drones and ballistic missiles of the Iskander-M or the North Korean KN-23 model struck 22 different locations, and debris fell in three areas, according to the statement.
The attacks came as Russia continued its campaign against Ukraine's energy grid ahead of winter. Attacks on energy facilities across the country overnight and on the morning of Oct. 17 left some homes without power, the Energy Ministry said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky described Russia's latest attack as "one of the largest strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure." Russian forces targeted more than 15 key power generation and transmission facilities across Ukraine, he said.
"At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelensky said on social media, calling on Washington to pressure Moscow through a "sanctions blackout."
"Financial rewards for (Russian President Vladimir) Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. We must not give up ground."
In Kharkiv Oblast, Russian attacks killed a man and a woman, aged 58 and 71. Another 41 people were injured or suffered from stress, including three children, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
Four women and three men were injured in Sumy Oblast in Russian drone attacks, local authorities reported.
Russian attacks near the city of Nikopol in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast killed a 74-year-old woman and injured two men over the past day, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. One more man was killed in Dnipro, the regional center, after Russian forces targeted an industrial facility.
Russia launched one of its largest attacks on central Vinnytsia Oblast since the start of the full-scale invasion, targeting civilian and critical infrastructure with drones and injuring six people, Governor Natalia Zabolotna said.
Russian forces targeted civilian infrastructure in Odesa Oblast, injuring at least four people, Governor Oleh Kiper said.
Two people were killed in Kramatorsk in Donetsk Oblast, Governor Vadym Filashkin said. Fifteen more people were injured in the region over the past day.
Russian troops also attacked Zaporizhzhia Oblast, injuring six people, said Ivan Fedorov, head of the Zaporizhzhia Oblast Defense Council.
In Kherson Oblast, Russian forces targeted 31 towns and villages, including the regional center of Kherson. One person was killed, and at least 19 others were injured, including children, Governor Oleksandr Prokudin reported.

articles.title: Russian Overnight Attack Kills Civilians, Targets Energy Facilities Across Ukraine
articles.body:
Russia struck Ukraine overnight with ballistic and cruise missiles as well as hundreds of drones, killing civilians and damaging residential buildings, Ukrainian authorities said on October 17.
The attacks also disrupted power supply in several regions, officials said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the barrage "one of [Russia's] largest attacks on Ukraine's energy sector," adding that more than 15 "critical power generation and transmission facilities" were targeted across the country.
Writing on X on October 17, he said that the worst-hit areas included Lutsk, Rivne, Zhytomyr, Vinnytsya, Shepetivka, Slavuta, and Netishyn, and that "energy facilities in the Kharkiv, Kyiv, Dnipro, and other regions were also hit."
"The Russians have scaled up their anti-energy operation and are trying to stretch our reserves and repair capabilities as thin as possible," Zelenskyy wrote. "Between 7 p.m. yesterday and 7 a.m. today alone, more than 320 jet-powered and gasoline-powered 'shaheds,' along with loitering munitions, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles, were used against our energy sector, our cities, and our communities."
Russia launched four Kalibr cruise missiles and 332 attack drones, including 31 jet-powered drones, as well as Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles and Kh-22/32 cruise missiles, according to Ukraine's air force.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 293 aerial targets, including all four Kalibr missiles and 289 drones, the air force said. Impacts were recorded at 22 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at three others.
In the southern city of Kherson, a Russian air strike on the Korabelniy district killed a 64-year-old emergency medical services driver, regional military administration head Yaroslav Shanko said.
In Slovyansk, in the eastern Donetsk region, Russian forces struck a residential neighborhood with FAB-250 aerial bombs in the early hours of the morning, hitting two apartment buildings, according to local authorities.
One person was killed and 10 others were wounded in the attack, four of whom were hospitalized. Search-and-rescue operations were under way, with people potentially trapped beneath the rubble of both buildings.
Eight apartment buildings were damaged, two of them partially destroyed. A total of 16 people were wounded in Slovyansk over the past 24 hours, including a 17-year-old girl. Vehicles and municipal equipment were also damaged.
The strikes also placed further strain on Ukraine's electricity system. National grid operator Ukrenergo announced emergency power cuts in several regions, saying previously published outage schedules would not apply in areas affected by the measures.
Energy workers were working to restore supplies, and authorities urged consumers who still had electricity to use it sparingly.
In Vinnytsya, the regional capital in central Ukraine, Russian attacks left the city without electricity, Mayor Serhiy Morhunov said. Officials were assessing the extent of the damage, while critical infrastructure switched to backup power.
The latest barrage came as US President Donald Trump announced that he had waived nearly all substantive sanctions, tariffs, and restrictions included in a bipartisan law aimed at pressuring Russia to end its war against Ukraine, prompting sharp criticism from Ukraine advocates and lawmakers from both parties who say the move undermines efforts to force Moscow to negotiate.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's General Staff said on October 17 that Ukrainian forces remained in control of the eastern town of Dobropillia, rejecting a claim by Russian President Vladimir Putin a day earlier that Russian forces had captured the town.
Kyiv also disputed Moscow's claim that Russian forces had seized more than 1,800 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory and 92 settlements since September 1, Reuters reported.

articles.title: In space, no one hears Zelensky scream: No euros can buy Kiev options in orbit
articles.body:
In space, no one hears Zelensky scream: No euros can buy Kiev options in orbit
No matter how European leaders pledge to support Ukraine come hell or high water and let the taxpayers foot the bill, the cold hard fact is that there are things no euros can buy, such as US intelligence and satellite communications.
Kiev’s critical reliance on American space capabilities came to the fore this week when the long-standing feud between US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Zelensky flared up again. Trump, who had struck a diesel supply deal with Russia, called Zelensky a hindrance to peace who should be replaced. Zelensky called Trump a weakling who had betrayed Ukraine, if not in those exact terms.
According to lamentations from Kiev corroborated by media reporting, the White House put a chokehold on the Zelensky government by suspending early warning about incoming Russian ballistic missiles and temporarily suspending access to Starlink satellite internet for fast-moving objects – such as drones used in Kiev’s “middle strike” operations inside what Washington recognizes as part of Ukraine.
It’s not like Kiev was not warned. During a meeting in Miami last week, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly told the Ukrainians the diesel deal announcement was coming and that Kiev should not have ignored Trump’s multiple requests to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Accounts shared with Axios and Reuters suggest the Americans were polite enough not to say “what a nice deal to get intelligence and internet you have; it would be a shame if something happened to it.” But they mentioned “all that the US has done for Ukraine.” The Ukrainians did take it as a threat.
Here are the alternatives Kiev would have, should Trump push the issue further.
No match for US intelligence
Intelligence that European NATO members can provide is a far cry from what the US has been delivering for years. Already, early warning about Russian ballistic missile launches has stopped coming, just as Zelensky is complaining.
The US operates the Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS), whose backbone is six geosynchronous orbit satellites equipped with thermal sensors that detect launch signatures, complemented by two active and two reserve payloads in a highly elliptical orbit.
SBIRS helps identify and estimate the trajectory of a weapon, but has limited ability to track missiles after the intensive boost phase. But knowing one is incoming helps ground and airborne radar systems that guide interceptor missiles.
Other NATO members rely on SBIRS intelligence and never thought they would need their own alternative.
Satellites operated by the US National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) and the Air Force’s electronic reconnaissance aircraft, such as the RC-135U Combat Sent, also collect intelligence about Russian air defense systems. It’s unclear how much data it shares with Kiev, but the media has said the US helps plan Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia to minimize Moscow’s ability to intercept.
European NATO members do have some similar capabilities, including France’s three CERES electronic-intelligence satellites, the UK’s three RC-135W Rivet Joint aircraft, and Germany’s SARah radar-reconnaissance space program, but there is only so much they can do to measure up to the world’s largest military spender.
OneWeb not to rule them all
On the connectivity side, Starlink and its military twin Starshield remain the most capable today. It has over 11,000 satellites in low Earth (LEO) orbit that can use lasers to route traffic between each other, boosting their bandwidth.
The Starlink Mini terminal weighs just 1.1 kg and has an integrated antenna, making it usable even on even smaller military drones. Even larger variants are compact, which makes them harder to spot, and they typically consume under 100 watts of power – both valuable features in frontline applications.
The most direct non-US alternative is Eutelsat OneWeb, which already complements Starlink access in Ukraine. It only has 600+ satellites in its constellation, but nevertheless offers a high-speed connection.
However, OneWeb’s orbital component “remains rooted in an outdated architecture and technology conceived a decade ago, without any evolution of its underlying design,” Christian Freiherr von der Ropp, an independent satellite consultant, told Reuters.
OneWeb ground hardware is likewise no match for Starlink in price, size, or appetite for energy. The relatively small Hughes HL1100W terminal weighs over 10 kg and consumes around 130 watts, though there are efforts to produce smaller and less power-hungry equipment.
Kymeta Corporation announced a OneWeb terminal in March whose 100-watt consumption it said was optimized for mobile platforms. Its “compact and lightweight design” means it weighs less than 11 kg, and the producer itself is Redmond, Washington.
Dark horses in orbit
In September, EU co-founder Luxembourg announced the successful launch of the final three of a planned 13 satellites of its O3b mPOWER communication system. The low number is misleading, since the constellation is being positioned in medium Earth orbit and requires fewer satellites for coverage.
The trade off is latency, which is higher by an order of magnitude compared to LEO-based systems, but Luxembourg’s system is still good enough for some military applications and is used by NATO.
O3b mPOWER’s potential for Ukraine’s war effort is limited due to its coverage, which is between 50° north latitude and 50° south latitude. Luxembourg is right on the northern border of the band, but a large part of Ukraine, including Kiev, is outside of it. As they say, geography is destiny.
GOVSATCOM, the EU’s program to band together communication satellites owned by several member states, is somewhat of a dark horse, but public data suggests its capabilities are too limited to replace Starlink.
Amazon Leo is currently in limited preview, but it’s hard to expect an American company and a major Pentagon contractor to publicly defy Trump at Brussels’ call. Russia’s in-development Rassvet system is obviously not an option.
The EU’s proposed IRIS² system is years away from being operational, as is Canada’s Telesat Lightspeed.
In short, should Ukraine lose Starlink, in the short term Europe cannot replace it, as EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas acknowledged on Friday.

articles.title: Zelensky Says Starlink Still Not Fully Restored, Disrupting Russian Drone Interceptions and Food Deliveries to Frontline Troops
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Friday, Oct. 16, that Ukraine’s military Starlink satellite communications capabilities have still not been fully restored, warning that restrictions on the US-provided system had prevented Ukrainian forces from shooting down Russian jet-powered drones and disrupted essential supplies to frontline soldiers.
Speaking at a press conference in Brussels after meeting EU leaders, Zelensky said the restrictions were gradually being reversed but that Ukraine had not regained the full operating capabilities needed to protect civilians against Russia’s increasingly fast attack drones.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Has the speed been fully restored to what it was before? No. Is the speed being restored now? Yes,” Zelensky said.
The president’s comments came as a Reuters investigation raised fresh questions about Washington’s role in restrictions affecting Ukraine’s military-grade Starshield network, operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
Zelensky said Ukraine’s Defense Ministry remained in daily contact with partners to resolve the disruption and restore the capabilities Ukrainian forces previously possessed.
He revealed that he had received information suggesting the White House had contacted SpaceX about reversing the restrictions.
“Our partners told me there was a signal from the White House administration to SpaceX to restore this,” Zelensky said.
Trump Halts Sweeping Russia Sanctions, Citing US National Interest
“I don’t know whether that’s true or not. If it is, we are very grateful.”
Despite the reported intervention, the Zelensky made clear that the problem had not been fully resolved.
Russian Shaheds outpace restricted Ukrainian interceptors
Zelensky offered a detailed explanation of how Starlink restrictions undermined Ukraine’s defense against jet-powered Shahed drones, which Russia has increasingly deployed against Ukrainian cities.
“We use Starlink to intercept jet-powered Shaheds that come and strike our civilians and kill our families,” he said.
“We use special interceptors that move at very high speeds – interceptor drones that operate specifically with Starlink.”
According to Zelensky, Ukraine’s satellite terminals were subjected to restrictions that prevented high-speed drones from maintaining the connections required for their missions.
“Starlink was not switched off. The speed was reduced,” he said.
“And when the speed was reduced, we were unable to shoot down some of the Shaheds.”
Zelensky said Russian jet-powered drones were flying at speeds exceeding 400 km/h (249 mph), while Ukrainian Starlink-equipped systems had faced a movement-speed threshold of approximately 70 km/h (43 mph).
The consequences, Zelensky said, were particularly serious because the affected drones were intended to stop Russian attacks before they reached civilian areas.
“We were unable to use a tool to protect civilians,” he said.
“This is very painful and unpleasant.”
Starlink restrictions disrupted food and water deliveries to Ukrainian troops
Zelensky said the Starlink restrictions also disrupted food and water deliveries to Ukrainian soldiers holding frontline positions under constant Russian drone surveillance, where conventional supply vehicles cannot safely reach them.
“Our most important thing is people,” Zelensky said.
“Food and water are delivered to our soldiers, who spend weeks and months on the front line, using drones equipped with Starlink,” he said.
Those operations require drones capable of traveling at high speeds, making satellite communication restrictions particularly disruptive.
Zelensky said the limitations interfered with these deliveries while simultaneously weakening Ukraine’s ability to intercept drones targeting civilians.
“They were cutting off our logistics and the protection of the civilian population,” he said.
Ukraine seeks independence from US-controlled military technology
Zelensky acknowledged that Ukraine continues to rely on US intelligence for early warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches, despite receiving intelligence from dozens of other countries.
“Regarding ballistic missiles, specifically information about their launches, we receive that information from the United States,” he explained.
“As you can see, there are many challenges, particularly those related to ballistic missiles.”
Zelensky said Ukraine was working to reduce such vulnerabilities by strengthening its own technological capabilities and cooperation with European partners.
“We are working on every possible option to make Ukraine as independent as possible,” he said.

articles.title: Russian troops liberate 12 communities in Ukraine operation over week — top brass
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. Russian troops liberated 12 communities in the Kharkov and Zaporozhye Regions and the Donetsk People’s Republic over the week of October 10-16, including two communities during the past 24 hours in the special military operation in Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"Last week, Battlegroup North units took control of the settlements of Lukashovo, Lobanovka, Reznikovo, Kupino, Nefyodovka and Chernoye and yesterday they established control of the settlements of Varvarovka and Nikolayevka in the Kharkov Region through active and decisive operations. <…> During the week, Battlegroup Center units liberated the settlements of Novotroitskoye, Petrovskoye and Lidino in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said in a statement.
"Over the past week, Battlegroup East units continued their advance deep into the enemy’s defenses and liberated the settlement of Nikolskoye in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry reported.
Russian troops deliver eight precision strikes on Ukrainian military sites over week
Russian troops delivered one massive and seven combined strikes by precision weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles on Ukrainian military-industrial facilities, logistics and telecommunications centers and ammunition depots over the week, the ministry reported.
"On October 10-16, 2026, the Russian Armed Forces delivered one massive and seven combined strikes, hitting military-industrial enterprises, logistics and telecommunications centers, transport infrastructure facilities used to support the Ukrainian army’s operations, sites producing and storing unmanned aerial vehicles, ammunition and materiel depots, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries," the ministry said.
Russian troops delivered strikes over the week, degrading some infrastructure facilities of Ukrainian ports used to receive and store military supplies, it said.
"In addition, some infrastructure facilities of Ukraine’s ports used to receive, store and distribute military cargo were degraded," the ministry said.
Russian troops struck 15 dry cargo ships involved in the delivery of Western weapons and military hardware to the Ukrainian army over the week, the ministry reported.
"During the week, 15 dry cargo ships involved in the delivery of Western weapons, military hardware, fuel and equipment for the needs of the Ukrainian army were hit," the ministry said.
Russia’s Battlegroup North thwarts Ukrainian attempts to break out of encirclement in Kharkov area
Russia’s Battlegroup North thwarted all the Ukrainian army’s attempts during the past week to break out of the encirclement in the Kharkov Region, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup North units continued tightening the ring of encirclement of enemy formations in the northeast of the Kharkov Region and expanding the outer area of control. <…> All the enemy’s attempts to break out of the encirclement were thwarted," the ministry said.
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicts over 1,675 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicted more than 1,675 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed five enemy armored combat vehicles in its areas of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
During the past week in the Kharkov and Sumy Regions, Battlegroup North units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of six mechanized brigades, two motorized infantry brigades, two airmobile brigades, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army, four territorial defense brigades and a National Guard brigade," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,675 personnel, five armored combat vehicles, 82 motor vehicles, three field artillery guns and eight electronic warfare stations in the areas of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup North over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicts over 1,550 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicted more than 1,550 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 18 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"During the past week, Battlegroup West units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on formations of two mechanized brigades, an assault brigade of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and two territorial defense brigades," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,550 personnel, 18 armored combat vehicles, 94 motor vehicles, 12 field artillery guns and 11 electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicts over 1,155 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicted more than 1,155 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed nine enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"Over the past week, Battlegroup South units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, a motorized infantry brigade, a mountain assault brigade, an airmobile brigade, an unmanned systems brigade of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and a territorial defense brigade," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,155 personnel, nine armored combat vehicles, 198 motor vehicles, 13 field artillery guns and two electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicts over 2,740 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted more than 2,740 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 37 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
Over the past week, Battlegroup Center units "inflicted losses on formations of four mechanized brigades, a jaeger brigade, an airborne brigade of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and three National Guard brigades," the ministry said.
Overall, the Ukrainian army lost more than 2,740 personnel, 37 armored combat vehicles, 76 motor vehicles, 11 field artillery guns and 11 electronic warfare stations in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicts over 1,695 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 1,695 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed seven enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
During the past week, Battlegroup East units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of a mechanized brigade, an assault brigade, three air assault brigades, three assault regiments of the Ukrainian army and two marine infantry brigades," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,695 personnel, seven armored combat vehicles, 53 motor vehicles, three field artillery guns and two electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminates 240 Ukrainian troops in week
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminated roughly 240 Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy armored combat vehicle in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"Last week, Battlegroup Dnepr units improved their tactical position and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, a mountain assault brigade, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade," the ministry said.
"As many as 240 [Ukrainian] military personnel, an armored combat vehicle, 116 motor vehicles, five artillery guns and nine electronic warfare stations were destroyed," the ministry reported.
Russian air defenses intercept 5,695 Ukrainian UAVs, four cruise missiles over week
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 5,695 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and four Flamingo cruise missiles over the week, the ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down seven guided aerial bombs, two rockets of the US-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket system, four Flamingo long-range cruise missiles, a Neptune long-range missile and 5,695 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said.
Tally of Ukrainian army’s losses
Overall, the Russian Armed Forces have destroyed 674 Ukrainian combat aircraft, 284 helicopters, 263,235 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 31,251 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,790 multiple rocket launchers, 36,738 field artillery guns and mortars and 74,686 special military motor vehicles since the start of the special military operation, the ministry reported.

articles.title: Trump Waives Graham Act Sanctions On Russia Before They Take Effect
articles.body:
WASHINGTON -- US President Donald Trump has waived nearly all substantive sanctions, tariffs, and restrictions included in a bipartisan law aimed at pressuring Russia to end its war against Ukraine, prompting sharp criticism from Ukraine advocates and lawmakers from both parties who say the move undermines efforts to force Moscow to negotiate.
In an executive order signed late on October 16, Trump said withholding the measures was in the national interest of the United States. The order came just two days before the sanctions package was due to take effect on October 18.
The legislation, known as the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, was signed into law by Trump in September. It was named posthumously for Republican Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, a prominent congressional supporter of Ukraine who died on July 11.
The law was designed to give the administration additional leverage over Russian President Vladimir Putin by authorizing tariffs of up to 100 percent on major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, including China and India, and providing for sanctions targeting Russian officials, financial institutions, and the country's so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent existing restrictions.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy responded on October 17 by saying that it was an unfortunate decision to backtrack on the sanctions at a time when "pressure is needed"
"At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "This Act could have helped enormously -- and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters."
"Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine -- right before winter," he said. "Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating. Pressure is needed to stop this. A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin -- all of this only encourages him to keep attacking."
Trump's decision to waive the measures has raised questions about whether his administration intends to use the economic pressure Congress sought to place on Moscow to compel an end to the war.
In the order, Trump said the legislation authorized him to waive the application of sanctions provisions against foreign individuals. He said he had submitted a certification to Congress that issuing the waiver was in the national interest.
The law also requires the administration to provide a report explaining the basis for that certification. The report must be submitted in unclassified form, although it may include a classified annex.
The White House has not publicly detailed, in the material provided for this report, the substantive justification for waiving the law's major provisions.
'A Cruel Policy Choice'
Mykola Murskyj, director of advocacy at Razom for Ukraine, a US-based nonprofit supporting Ukraine, told RFE/RL that Trump had squandered an opportunity to increase pressure on Putin.
"Trump squandered a golden opportunity to bring peace to Ukraine," Murskyj said.
He said lawmakers had spent months building bipartisan support for the legislation, which included tariffs on countries buying Russian oil, restrictions on purchases of Russian sovereign debt, and limits on new investments in Russia.
"All that has been erased in a late-night order Friday from the White House," Murskyj said.
He also questioned the duration of the waivers. "Shockingly, these waivers don't even have an expiration date," he said.
Razom condemned the decision in a separate statement, saying that refusing to use the tools available to pressure Russia was a deliberate policy choice.
"Lacking the tools to end this war would be a tragedy. Having them and refusing to use them is a cruel policy choice," said Daniel Balson, Razom's director of advocacy.
Balson said the legislation had been painstakingly negotiated by a bipartisan group of senators working with White House officials over several months before winning substantial support in both chambers of Congress.
"Today's implementation order signals to the Kremlin that it can continue its invasion," he said, adding that Ukrainians would continue fighting despite mounting humanitarian and energy challenges.
In the week before the waiver, Russia reportedly launched more than 700 drones, along with ballistic and cruise missiles, against Ukrainian cities and power plants.
Questions Over Justification, Deadlines
The decision has also raised questions about what explanation the Trump administration provided to Congress for setting aside the sanctions and tariff provisions.
Max Meizlish, a former official at the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control who is now deputy director of the Center on Economic and Financial Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told RFE/RL that the administration's justification was now a central issue.
"The question now is what substantive justification the administration provided Congress for waiving virtually every major sanctions and tariff provision of legislation that passed with bipartisan support," Meizlish said.
Under the law, the administration must submit a written certification that the waiver is in the national interest, along with a report explaining the basis for that determination. The reporting requirements are intended to provide Congress with an account of the reasoning behind the administration's decision.
Separately, Section 113 of the law sets out requirements for providing written justification to relevant congressional committees in connection with the imposition of tariffs. Sources familiar with the matter told RFE/RL that the administration had missed an October 8 deadline related to those requirements.
The waiver also follows a separate decision by Trump to permit Russian diesel sales amid concerns over rising fuel prices and global supply shortages.
Trump said last week that Russia could immediately supply 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and then 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."
The waiver comes as the administration seeks to bring down US fuel prices ahead of November's midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress. Energy prices have also been affected by the US war in Iran.
It has drawn criticism from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers who had supported the Graham legislation and urged the president to implement it fully, as well as from Ukraine and its European allies. Zelenskyy called it "a gift" for Putin.
Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat and co-author of the bill, accused Trump of siding with Putin and the networks that sustain Russia's war effort.
"Donald Trump confirms again that he stands on the side of a bloodthirsty thug and the enablers of Russia's war machine," Blumenthal wrote on social media, arguing the decision ran counter to the views of most Americans, members of Congress, and European allies.
"These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," he added.
Republican Representative Don Bacon also criticized the president's move, saying: "The President is prolonging the war, not ending it."
On October 16, Representative Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, introduced bipartisan legislation to block Trump's proposed deal to buy diesel from Russia.
The deal "will hand Putin millions of dollars to continue slaughtering Ukrainian civilians with impunity," Meeks said, urging Congress to pass the legislation.

articles.title: Russia Hits 15 Energy Sites in Massive Strike, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Russian forces launched one of their largest coordinated assaults against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, striking more than 15 critical electricity generation and transmission facilities across multiple provinces, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Saturday, Oct. 17.
The president reported that emergency restoration operations are underway across the country, mobilizing municipal utility workers and specialized engineering crews from domestic power companies to restore severed power supplies.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“On the eve, the Russians delivered one of their largest strikes against Ukrainian energy: more than 15 critical electricity generation and energy transmission facilities in various regions of Ukraine were attacked,” Zelensky stated.
“Restoration work is ongoing, involving all necessary services and all available resources of Ukrainian energy companies. I thank everyone working virtually non-stop to restore power.”
Regional impact and grid dispersion tactics
Zelensky highlighted that the most severe disruptions to municipal electricity networks were recorded in northwestern and central urban centers, specifically identifying Lutsk, Rivne, Zhytomyr, Vinnytsia, Shepetivka, Slavuta, and Netishyn.
Additional kinetic strikes and falling debris damaged energy installations across Kharkiv region, Kyiv region, and Dnipropetrovsk region alongside other administrative jurisdictions.
According to the president, the operational breadth of the assault reflects an intentional Russian doctrine engineered to exhaust municipal repair reserves and disperse domestic technical response teams ahead of freezing winter temperatures.
EU Tasks Commission to Bridge Ukraine’s €70B Funding Gap
“The Russians scaled up their anti-energy operation and are trying to disperse our reserves and recovery capacity to the maximum,” Zelensky said.
Between 7:00 p.m. on Friday and 7:00 a.m. on Saturday, Russian forces deployed more than 320 strike drones against Ukraine’s civil power networks, municipal infrastructure, and residential settlements.
The wave comprised a mix of turbojet-powered and conventional piston-engine Shahed loitering munitions, loitering compact cruise weapons, alongside cruise and ballistic missiles.
“And although our warriors manage to shoot down a significant portion, the scale and continuity of Russian strikes – specifically against energy – unfortunately has many negative consequences,” Zelensky noted.
Push for European support
Zelensky confirmed that European partner nations have assembled new military and energy assistance packages to reinforce Ukrainian defenses, expressing gratitude for European solidarity following high-level summits in Brussels.
Concurrently, the president addressed policymakers and the public in the US, criticizing recent decisions in Washington to waive statutory economic sanctions and tariffs targeting the Russia.
“It is important that everyone in America also sees what is actually happening,” Zelensky emphasized.
“At a time when the Russians delivered such a massive strike against our energy, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham law, which was supposed to introduce truly effective pressure on Russia to end this war.”
The presidential statement referred to the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which US President Donald Trump signed into law on Sept. 18 but waived via executive order on Friday, Oct. 16, just 48 hours before mandatory 500 percent tariffs on Russian imports and 100 percent duties on third-party petroleum buyers were set to take effect.
“This law could – and still can! – help greatly. But the law needs to actually work, and every vote for this matters,” Zelensky urged, noting that relieving economic pressure incentivizes further aggression.
“Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating,” Zelensky stated.
“Pressure is needed to stop this. An American sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, monetary rewards for [Russian President Vladimir] Putin – all of this only encourages him to strike further. We must not surrender positions; we must try to end the war. End it, rather than give Putin every reason to prolong it indefinitely.”

articles.title: Moscow welcomes Trump’s sanctions waiver as Ukraine voices alarm
articles.body:
Russia on Saturday welcomed U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision to waive new sanctions targeting Moscow, calling it a historic move as Ukraine warned that easing economic pressure would encourage Russian President Vladimir Putin to continue the war.
Trump signed an executive order Friday suspending the application of sanctions provisions under the Lindsey Graham Act, a law designed to increase pressure on Russia’s energy and defense sectors, its officials and the network of tankers Moscow uses to circumvent Western restrictions.
The decision comes as Russian forces intensify attacks on Ukrainian cities and diplomatic efforts led by Washington remain deadlocked, raising concerns among Kyiv and its European allies that the Trump administration is easing pressure on Moscow without securing meaningful concessions.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special envoy for investment and economic cooperation, praised the decision on social media, describing the suspension of the law as an “important and truly historic moment.”
Dmitriev argued that the sanctions would have caused serious damage to the U.S. economy and global markets. The Kremlin and Putin had not publicly commented on the decision as of Saturday.
The waiver followed an arrangement between Trump and Putin under which Moscow agreed to release substantial quantities of diesel onto global markets amid mounting pressure on fuel prices. Trump’s decision to suspend the new measures marks a diplomatic gain for Russia as Washington struggles to broker an end to the war.
The Graham Act, named after the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, was designed to tighten restrictions on Russia’s energy and defense industries, officials linked to Putin and its so-called shadow fleet of tankers. It also included provisions targeting countries that continue to buy Russian oil and gas.
Trump’s order suspends the application of the new measures under a national-interest waiver. It does not automatically remove sanctions imposed on Russia under earlier U.S. measures.
The decision has intensified concerns in Kyiv that Washington could weaken its leverage over Moscow while Russian forces continue their offensive.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the waiver Saturday, arguing that easing sanctions would reward Russia despite its continued attacks.
“A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin, all of this only encourages him to keep attacking,” Zelenskyy said on social media, urging Ukraine’s allies to maintain pressure on Moscow.
The sanctions decision came as Russia stepped up its attacks on Ukraine, including repeated strikes on the capital, Kyiv, as the war enters its fifth year.
Russian forces struck the southern city of Kherson on Saturday, killing one person and wounding 22, local officials said. The attack underscored the continuing toll of the war even as Washington pursues negotiations.
The conflict, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions. Russian forces occupy large areas of eastern and southern Ukraine, and Putin has repeatedly vowed to seize the remaining territory Moscow claims in eastern Ukraine.
Speaking to military leaders Friday while wearing military uniform, Putin said he saw a positive trend in the operations of Russian forces and reiterated that capturing the rest of the Donetsk region remained a major objective.
“Undoubtedly, one of the main objectives remains the liberation of the Donetsk People’s Republic,” Putin said, using the Kremlin’s term for the Ukrainian region.
Russian strikes have intensified in recent weeks, putting additional pressure on Ukrainian air defenses as the country prepares for another winter of war. Kyiv has struggled to intercept incoming missiles and drones while seeking additional defensive systems from its allies.
Putin’s remarks signaled that Moscow intends to continue its military campaign despite diplomatic efforts to secure a ceasefire.
European leaders responded to the growing uncertainty over Washington’s approach by reaffirming their support for Ukraine and calling for continued economic pressure on Russia.
Zelenskyy met European leaders in Brussels on Friday during a European Union summit, seeking sustained financial and military assistance as relations between Kyiv and Washington deteriorated.
European Council President António Costa warned against easing pressure on Moscow while Russian forces continued their attacks.
“This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions,” Costa said. “Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure.”
European leaders have argued that maintaining sanctions and strengthening Ukraine’s defenses are necessary to persuade Russia to accept a meaningful ceasefire and negotiate an end to the war.
The EU has also signaled that it intends to maintain its restrictions on Moscow while preparing further measures.
Zelenskyy has sought additional air defense systems, support for Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and continued funding to sustain the country’s defense effort. His appeal came as European governments weighed how to maintain assistance amid uncertainty over the future direction of U.S. policy.
The European response reflects growing concern that Washington’s willingness to ease sanctions could undermine the pressure intended to bring Putin to the negotiating table.
U.S.-led negotiations have yet to produce a breakthrough, with disputes over territory, security guarantees and the terms of a possible ceasefire continuing to obstruct progress.
Trump has expressed frustration with both Putin and Zelenskyy over the lack of progress toward ending the conflict. His increasingly strained relationship with the Ukrainian leader has added to concerns in Kyiv that Washington could press Ukraine to make concessions while offering Moscow economic relief.
The sanctions waiver has heightened those fears, particularly as Ukraine faces intensified Russian bombardments and questions over the reliability of some U.S.-provided military and intelligence support.
For Ukraine, the immediate concern is that easing economic pressure could give Russia greater room to sustain its military campaign. For European governments, the decision raises questions about how to maintain a unified strategy if Washington takes a more conciliatory approach toward Moscow.
Russia’s public celebration of the waiver reflects the potential diplomatic value of the move for Putin, even as the Kremlin continues to pursue its territorial objectives by force.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Starlink speed restrictions hamper Ukraine’s military, humanitarian operations
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday that the Starlink system had not been completely switched off in Ukraine, but speed restrictions affected the country's ability to use it for certain military and humanitarian purposes.
Speaking at a briefing on the sidelines of the EU leaders’ summit in Brussels, Zelesnkyy said the Defense Ministry remained in contact with partners and that he received indications from the White House that services would be fully restored.
He claimed Ukraine was not using Starlink to conduct deep-strikes against targets inside Russia, but relied on the system to operate interceptor drones against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
He said the restrictions also affected Ukraine's ability to carry out medium-range strikes against military targets.
Starlink-enabled drones, he said, were used to deliver food and water to Ukrainian personnel in positions exposed to enemy drone attacks.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine receives information from the US specifically about Russian ballistic missile launches, while dozens of countries also share intelligence with Kyiv.
He said Ukraine receives PAC-2 and PAC-3 air defense missiles from the US through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, with European countries financing the deliveries.
“So it's no gift. It's not for free,” he said, acknowledging that Ukraine is not currently a priority destination for the missiles, as many are being sent to the Middle East.
The Ukrainian leader criticized the recent US-Russia diesel deal and the prospect of lifting sanctions, saying Kyiv had not been informed in advance.
Ukraine, he said, proposed an energy ceasefire and offered the US to provide Kyiv with anti-ballistic missiles to protect energy infrastructure for the duration of the arrangement. “Don't give too many. Give us for the period you'll need for the duration of the diesel deal. I have not received that,” he said.
Responding to Donald Trump’s remark that he was more difficult to deal with than Russian President Vladimir Putin, Zelenskyy said negotiating with the US president was easier than dealing with the Russian leader.
He said ending the war remained his priority but accused Putin of showing no genuine desire for negotiations. He warned that concessions on sanctions could eventually lead to broader agreements with Moscow, including in the energy, chemical industry and banking sectors.
“In my view, we cannot perceive diesel deals, these arrangements. We cannot accept them because then there will be gas agreements. I'm sure of that,” he said.
Zelenskyy also rejected the notion that the war was solely about control of the Donbas region, saying Ukraine’s national existence was at stake. “The issue is not withdrawing from Donbas. It's the issue of our country's existence,” he said, arguing that Moscow’s objectives of the war extend beyond eastern Ukraine.
He said European countries understood the risks posed by Russia, and urged partners to continue supporting Kyiv.

articles.title: Zelenskyy urges EU not to ease sanctions against Russia during leaders' meeting
articles.body:
Burç Eruygur
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
 Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday urged the EU not to ease sanctions against Russia, stressing the need for a “strong” 22nd sanctions package from the 27-member union.
Speaking on the second day of an EU leaders’ summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy accused his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin of seeking to “drag out” the Ukraine war into next year, saying Europe must be ready for this.
“I urge you not to ease sanctions against Russia or anyone linked to it. Putin uses every trick he can find to get money for making more weapons,” Zelenskyy said, noting Ukraine has warned that sanctions relief will result in others taking advantage.
The Ukrainian leader argued that the diesel deal between the US and Russia will never be enough to offset the impact of the situation in the Strait of Hormuz on global markets, but will rather “put more money straight into Putin’s pocket to fund this war.”
He stressed the need for a strong 22nd EU sanctions package, particularly calling for sanctions against all involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles, advanced communications systems and drones.
Zelenskyy said the financial cost of the ongoing conflict for Ukraine will be €155 billion next year and it needs at least €70 billion more for spending, including in terms of defense purchases.
He stressed the need to deal with Russian frozen assets, as well as called on European leaders to use every opportunity to strengthen air defense, emphasizing the need for a winter package consisting of 300 Patriot interceptors against Russian ballistic missiles.
“We are grateful that the EU is moving toward us. Four EU accession clusters have already been opened this year. And we need to open the remaining two by the end of the year. We are ready,” Zelenskyy said, calling on the union to keep Ukraine and Moldova's membership processes tied together.
Defining unity in Europe as a target for Russia, Zelenskyy said that in spite of disagreements and their differences, all of them seek a security system in Europe that “really works and can deal with today’s threats.”
“So, as we work now to finally stop Putin, to stop his war, we are doing this not just for Ukraine alone. We are working for security guarantees for all of Europe. For guarantees that this war will not be passed down to our children,” he said.
He expressed gratitude to those supporting Ukraine and those trying to keep Europe and the US together. “Putin will listen to America if America really turns up the heat on him and makes one thing clear -- either he chooses peace, or he gets no more money for his war,” he said.
Zelenskyy arrived in Brussels on Thursday to attend the European Council summit and hold a number of talks on the sidelines of the event.
Zelenskyy met with the presidents of the European Council and European Commission, as well as held talks with the Hungarian, Finnish and Swedish prime ministers on Friday.
On Thursday, he met his French counterpart Emmanuel Macron, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, Belgian King Philippe, and the prime ministers of Belgium, Denmark, and Poland.

articles.title: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as new US law takes effect
articles.body:
Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
- Published
Donald Trump has blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens.
The sanctions were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by Trump in September.
But the US president issued an executive order on Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US "national interest", prompting a backlash from US lawmakers. Zelensky said it was unfortunate the US has decided to "completely disregard" the sanctions.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel. Ukraine then accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.
Trump and Zelensky have exchanged sharp words about one another. Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy, giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.
It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes.
- Trump denies limiting Ukraine access to Starlink network 
  - Published16 hours ago
- Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC 
  - Published12 hours ago
Many of these provisions have now been waived by Trump.
Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev called the waiver "an important and truly historic moment".
Posting on X, he said the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage" primarily on the US and global market, and that economic cooperation benefits both nations.
Democrats including the Virginia Congressman Don Beyer have criticised the move, accusing Trump of capitulating to Moscow and turning his back on Kyiv and Zelensky.
"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer wrote on X.
The move is likely to draw further anger from Ukraine, where Zelensky has long stressed the need for stringent sanctions to limit funding Russia can use in its war effort.
Zelensky said on Saturday morning that the sanctions "could have helped enormously" and that the law was "supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end".
He pointed to Russian overnight attacks on 15 Ukrainian energy facilities that had caused power cuts in several regions and said: "Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine – right before winter."
Zelensky said was "important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening" on the ground.
He later told reporters that he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.
He also said negotiators Ukrainian spoke to their US counterparts on Friday and that both teams could meet next week.
Trump was initially criticised by Zelensky and Ukraine's European allies for temporarily suspending some US sanctions to import Russian diesel in a bid to bring down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.
Trump has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Middle East conflict, which has sent fuel costs soaring ahead of the US midterm elections. Rising inflation has soured Trump's standing with the American public.
Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.
A few days later, Trump claimed that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" to facilitate the export of Russian diesel.
Both nations have been intensively striking one another's energy infrastructure. Kyiv says this is to limit revenue for Russia's war machine, while Moscow claims it only targets facilities used by the Ukrainian military.
Zelensky initially expressed surprise at Trump's announcement, and said Kyiv would stop the strikes if Russia did the same. After three days which saw several fresh attacks from Russia, Kyiv resumed its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
This prompted scathing condemnation from Trump, who called the strikes a "disgrace". Zelensky replied that he was "only standing up for Ukraine's interests".
Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine.
Last week Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield missions, Ukraine said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks.
During the slowdown, Russia launched several deadly strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying these came with no prior warning.
Zelensky said on Friday that Starlink speeds had still not been fully restored.
Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing and deliberately slowing down Ukraine's Starlink network.
Ukrainian authorities have confirmed that at least nine people have been killed and around 60 injured in Russian strikes across the country over the past 24 hours.
They said an ambulance driver was killed and 20 others were injured in Russian strikes on the city of Kherson on Saturday morning.
Russia's defence ministry said it had targeted industries linked to Ukraine's defence industry - including steel works, an electrical sub-station and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.

The Ukrainians, who have relied heavily on Starlink during the conflict with Russia for battlefield communications and controlling drones, have been “terrified” by the slowdown of satellite internet provided by Elon Musk’s SpaceX company this week, the WSJ said.

Last month, Peskov warned that allowing Starlink to be used to facilitate strikes deep into Russian territory would be “a very harmful, potentially dangerous and misconceived step.”
The American authorities apparently don’t require consent from Musk to expand the coverage of Starlink’s military component, known as Starshield, for Ukraine. articles.title: Ukraine downed four thousand seven hundred air targets
articles.body:
Ukrainian air defences destroyed more than 4,700 drones and missiles during September while repelling large-scale Russian attacks, and neutralised more than 48,000 tactical uncrewed aerial vehicles over the same month, according to the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence.
The figures, attributed to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, break down into a pattern dominated overwhelmingly by one-way attack drones. Shahed-131 and Shahed-136 types accounted for 2,722 of the interceptions and the jet-powered Shahed-238 for a further 1,935, with 1,009 reconnaissance drones and 719 Lancet loitering munitions also brought down.
Missile interceptions made up a far smaller share of the total, with Ukrainian defences stopping 24 Kh-101 cruise missiles, 12 Kalibr cruise missiles, eight Iskander-M and KN-23 ballistic missiles, six Iskander-K cruise missiles, six Kh-59 and Kh-69 guided air-launched missiles, and eight Zircon anti-ship missiles. Another 86 S8000 Banderol missiles were destroyed.
The ministry said the targets were destroyed “through the efforts of aviation, surface-to-air missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defence Forces of Ukraine.”
On where the difficulty now lies, the department said: “Ballistic missiles remain a challenge for Ukraine’s air defense. At the same time, the enemy is increasingly using jet-powered drones that fly at speeds of around 400 km/h, reducing the time available to detect and intercept them.”
It added: “In addition, the enemy sends small groups of several jet-powered drones to different regions. To counter such targets, Ukraine uses aviation, among other means, and is developing innovative interception capabilities.”
Jet-powered Shaheds were shot down at nearly thirteen times the rate of every Russian missile type combined, which is a measure of how far the campaign has shifted away from missiles. A propeller-driven Shahed cruises at around 180 kilometres an hour and can be engaged by a gun truck, a helicopter or a cheap interceptor drone. At 400 kilometres an hour the engagement window halves, mobile fire groups lose much of their usefulness, and the problem starts to look more like intercepting a cruise missile than swatting a lawnmower.
Sending them in small packets to widely separated regions compounds the problem, because a defence designed around massed raids on a few cities has to be spread thinly to cover dispersed single-target attacks, and the aircraft Ukraine is using to run down the fast drones are the same F-16s and Mirages it needs for other tasks.
Evgeniy Khmara, the Ukrainian Defence Minister, raised munitions supply for the F-16 force in a recent conversation with German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius, saying deliveries help ensure their effectiveness in shooting down Russian drones. The two also discussed protection of critical infrastructure and the need for more air defence assets including interceptors for the IRIS-T system.
Britain’s contribution to this problem has been concentrated on the cheap end, which is where the arithmetic works. The Lightweight Multirole Missile, built by Thales at Belfast and known in Royal Navy service as Martlet, has been supplied in quantity for counter-drone use, and the company confirmed this week that it has quadrupled production capacity at the site. Gravehawk, the British and Danish funded system that puts Soviet air-to-air missiles into a shipping container with a British sensor fit, was developed specifically to give Ukraine more launchers without waiting for Western interceptor stocks.

It also authorised tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods imported from major purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas, potentially affecting countries including China and India.
The new restrictions were scheduled to take effect on Sunday, 18 October, but Trump's order suspends their implementation until the administration determines that further action is appropriate.
"I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States," Trump stated in the order.
The decision comes amid concerns that additional restrictions on Russian energy exports could drive global oil prices higher ahead of November's US midterm elections. Energy costs have already risen sharply amid the ongoing US-Israeli conflict with Iran, placing political pressure on the Trump administration.
The move was welcomed by Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's investment envoy, who described the suspension as an "important and truly historic moment".
Dmitriev argued that implementing the sanctions would have severely damaged international markets and economic relations between Russia and the United States.
In Washington, Democratic Representative Don Beyer accused Trump of undermining congressional efforts to hold Moscow accountable.
"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer said in a statement.
The suspension follows another controversial decision by Washington to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports in a claimed effort to reduce American and global fuel prices.
That agreement prompted criticism from a bipartisan group of US senators, including six Republicans, who warned that renewed energy revenues could help finance Russia's military operations in Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has similarly condemned the diesel arrangement, warning that additional revenue would flow into Russia while its invasion continues.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv have deteriorated further over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. Trump has repeatedly demanded that Ukraine halt the strikes, arguing that they contribute to higher international energy prices.
Following the collapse of a proposed energy ceasefire, Ukraine resumed refinery attacks on Thursday after Russian forces continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Trump subsequently described the Ukrainian operations as a "disgrace" and renewed his criticism of Zelenskyy.
Ukrainian officials have reported disruptions to satellite communications used for drone operations, while Reuters reported, citing unnamed US and Western officials, that an order to restrict the Starshield system originated inside the White House.
Trump has denied personally ordering the restrictions and has rejected claims that Washington halted intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

Zelenskyy confirms Starlink speed restrictions hindered interception of jet-powered Shaheds
Ukraine was unable to intercept jet-powered Shahed drones to protect civilians because Starlink connection speeds had been reduced.
Source: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, speaking after meetings on the sidelines of the EU leaders' summit on 15-16 October, as reported by European Pravda's correspondent in Brussels
Details: Zelenskyy added that the reduction in Starlink speeds had also prevented Ukraine from striking military targets in occupied territories and delivering water and food to Ukrainian troops.

"We use [Starlink] to intercept jet-powered Shaheds that strike our civilians and kill our families. We use specialised interceptors that move at high speeds. Interceptor drones that operate specifically with Starlink," Zelenskyy said.
He pointed out that Starlink had not been switched off, but its connection speed had been reduced.
Quote: "When the speed was reduced, we were unable to intercept some of the jet-powered Shaheds… In other words, we were unable to use a tool to protect civilians. This is very painful and unpleasant."
Details: The president explained that jet-powered Shaheds fly at speeds of more than 400 km/h, while the Starlink restrictions had reduced the equipment speed available to Ukrainian troops intercepting Russian drones to 70 km/h.
Zelenskyy also said Ukraine uses Starlink for mid-range strikes against Russian military targets in temporarily occupied territories, but the reduction in connection speeds had prevented it from carrying out those operations as well.
In addition, Starlink is needed to deliver water and food to Ukrainian troops who spend weeks or months on the front line in areas under the Russians' full drone surveillance.
Zelenskyy noted that the Defence Ministry is in daily contact with the United States and had recently received information that the connection speed had been resumed.
"If that is the case, we are very grateful," the president added.
"We approached SpaceX and the White House to ask them to enable this capability," Zelenskyy said, noting that Ukraine has not received a positive response to its request.

articles.title: Beijing’s mediating power in international crises
articles.body:
Beijing’s mediating power in international crises
TEHRAN – In the new international order, the concept of “power” is no longer defined solely by the number of nuclear warheads, overseas military bases, or classical security alliances; rather, the new geometry of global power is shaped by the capacity of supply chains, currency exchanges, infrastructure investments, and economic interdependence.
Within this novel framework, China has managed to elevate its position from a mere trading power in the late twentieth century to a “structural actor in international crisis management”—an actor whose primary tools for intervening in crises are not missiles and sanctions, but economic integration and financial leverage.
The defining distinction of China’s approach to international crises is rooted in the theory of “developmental peace” as opposed to Western “liberal peace.” Beijing believes that the primary root of many geopolitical conflicts and security instabilities in the Middle East, Africa, and Central Asia lies not in a vacuum of Western democracy, but in poverty, a deficit of infrastructural development, and a lack of connection to global markets. Therefore, Beijing utilizes initiatives such as the Belt and Road and strategic energy partnerships as efficient tools to contain security shocks. When countries share tangible, mutual economic interests in the continuity of joint projects, the cost of escalating tensions and war increases dramatically for them.
A concrete and successful example of this strategy can be seen in Beijing’s historic mediation between Tehran and Riyadh. Leveraging its immense weight as the largest buyer of Persian Gulf energy and the primary trading partner of both countries, China provided an economic-strategic platform for a political agreement without the need for ideological alignments. This model demonstrated that Beijing’s crisis management levers are built on a commitment to mutual interests and non-interference in internal affairs—a factor that has made Beijing’s model attractive and acceptable among the countries of the Global South.
Furthermore, in complex crises such as the war in Ukraine or tensions surrounding maritime security, China has managed—by relying on its position as a core commodity buyer—to prevent devastating fractures in the global energy and food markets. China’s policy is to maintain a balance between trade with Russia while simultaneously safeguarding Western markets; a strategy that prevents the deepening of acute international deadlocks and the uncontrolled spread of crises into the global economy.
Ultimately, Beijing has demonstrated that economic power is not merely a source of wealth, but a decisive lever for containing shocks and moderating geopolitical behavior. Although China’s cautious policy and avoidance of direct security guarantees may appear to limit its role in certain acute crises, an undeniable reality remains: in the current post-hegemonic world, no major international crisis can be managed, sustainably resolved, or contained without considering Beijing’s capacities, considerations, and economic levers.
Mahdi Zolfaghari is an Associate Professor at the Department of Asian Studies in Allameh Tabataba’i University

articles.title: ‘Mother of all bombs’ will not rescue Trump from Iran war quagmire
articles.body:
‘Mother of all bombs’ will not rescue Trump from Iran war quagmire
TEHRAN — The possible use of America’s largest non-nuclear bomb against Iran may offer President Donald Trump a dramatic display of military power, but it is unlikely to resolve the strategic predicament facing Washington, analysts have warned, arguing that a spectacular explosion cannot substitute for a viable path out of a protracted war.
CNN reported on October 14 that the US military had developed strike plans that could include the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, commonly known as the “mother of all bombs,” against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if Trump orders a resumption of combat operations. The report cited multiple US officials familiar with the planning.
The prospect of deploying the weapon has raised questions about whether Washington is seeking a decisive military outcome or a dramatic action that could allow the president to declare victory without achieving his stated strategic objectives.
 
Even within US military planning circles, doubts have emerged over the weapon’s effectiveness in changing the course of the war, CNN reported. Reuters subsequently reported the story, noting that it had not independently verified CNN’s account.
A dramatic explosion, but what strategic result?
Dani Citrinowicz, a former Israeli military intelligence official, told the BBC that even using the “mother of all bombs” would not force Iran to surrender.
“Even the use of the [mother of all bombs] will not force Iran to surrender; although such an attack could have psychological effects and give Trump an opportunity to claim an imaginary victory,” he said, according to the quotation provided in the BBC-attributed report.
The assessment points to a fundamental distinction between the destructive power of a weapon and its ability to achieve political objectives. A strike can cause extensive damage without compelling an adversary to accept the attacker’s demands or bringing a conflict to a favourable conclusion.
Sina Azodi, director of the Middle East Studies Program at George Washington University, similarly questioned the strategic logic behind the reported option.
“Trump has a strange fascination with the symbolic use of American military power and wants to advertise it on his personal social media account through a grand spectacle and a massive explosion,” Azodi said, according to the quotation provided.
He also highlighted the weapon’s limitations against deeply buried targets, noting that it detonates in the air and has limited capacity to penetrate far underground.
The distinction matters because the MOAB was designed primarily to produce devastating blast effects over a broad surface area. It is not the same as a specialised penetrator designed to attack deeply buried, hardened facilities.
In an October 15 Al Jazeera explainer, military analyst Elijah Magnier said that using the MOAB would not guarantee the destruction of Iran’s deeply buried nuclear installations and could amount to little more than “political theatre.”
A weapon cannot resolve a strategic deadlock
The reported plans have emerged as the Trump administration faces pressure to demonstrate progress in a war that has failed to produce a clear political resolution.
In a CNN broadcast on October 15, senior national security reporter Zachary Cohen said Trump and his advisers had spent months discussing options that could be presented to the American public as a “definitive end” to the war.
Cohen said the military had been tasked with developing fresh strike options amid the absence of a diplomatic resolution and growing unpopularity of the conflict.
He also reported that the administration’s stated strategic goals remained unfulfilled.
That assessment raises a central question: what would a MOAB strike actually accomplish that previous attacks and existing military pressure have not?
The bomb’s destructive capacity is not in dispute. The uncertainty concerns whether its use would change Iran’s calculations, compel Tehran to capitulate or create conditions for a durable settlement.
A dramatic strike might generate powerful images and headlines. But if it does not achieve its declared objectives, it could instead expose the gap between the administration’s military capabilities and its ability to translate them into a political outcome.
The limits of spectacle
The MOAB is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal. Its deployment would represent a major escalation, but its size alone does not make it an appropriate weapon for every target.
CNN military analyst and retired Air Force Colonel Cedric Leighton explained in a broadcast on October 15 that the MOAB is designed to inflict damage over a large surface area, whereas Iran’s hardened and deeply buried nuclear facilities present a different targeting challenge.
He contrasted the MOAB with the Massive Ordnance Penetrator, a different weapon specifically designed to attack hardened underground targets.
Leighton also questioned the suitability of the aircraft required to deliver the MOAB for the Iranian operational environment.
The technical limitations reinforce the broader strategic problem. A weapon capable of producing an enormous explosion is not necessarily capable of destroying every intended target, still less of compelling a country to surrender.
A face-saving exit is not the same as victory
The most consequential possibility raised by the reporting is that the proposed strike could be intended partly to shape the political narrative of the war.
CNN’s reporting suggested that the administration was examining military options that could enable Trump to present the conflict as decisively concluded. Such a scenario would make the distinction between a battlefield achievement and a politically useful declaration of victory particularly important.
Citrinowicz’s assessment, as quoted by the BBC, captures that concern: the attack might provide an opportunity to claim victory without necessarily producing the underlying result.
This is the danger of treating military spectacle as a substitute for strategy. An attack can be visually overwhelming and still leave the fundamental dispute unresolved.
For Washington, the question is not simply whether the United States can deploy a powerful bomb. It is whether doing so would bring the war closer to an outcome that can be sustained politically and strategically.
 
The quagmire remains
The possibility of using the MOAB does not, by itself, demonstrate that Trump has authorised such an attack. The reports describe contingency planning, not a confirmed decision to deploy the weapon.
Reuters said it could not independently verify CNN’s initial report. CBS News separately reported on October 15 that the White House and Pentagon had prepared plans for possible use of the weapon if ordered by the president.
If the bomb fails to achieve its intended military objectives, the administration could find itself confronting the same fundamental problem after an even more dramatic attack. If it is used primarily to create the appearance of a decisive outcome, the gap between the declaration of victory and the realities on the ground could become harder to conceal.
The “mother of all bombs” may offer Trump a spectacle of overwhelming force. But an explosion, however large, cannot by itself deliver a political settlement, compel an adversary’s surrender or guarantee a way out of war.
The real test is not the size of the blast. It is whether the strategy behind it can produce an outcome that military power alone has so far failed to secure.
