Russian drones killed at least three people across Ukraine early on Friday, hit two shopping centers and temporarily knocked out power to over 1 million people nationwide after strikes on the energy grid, officials said.
A 71-year-old woman and a 58-year-old man died, and 12 more people were wounded in attacks on three districts of the eastern city of Kharkiv, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. He had earlier put the death toll at three.
Ukraine's energy ministry said its repair crews had restored power to over 1 million people who lost it in Russian attacks on Friday. It was unclear how many people were still without power.
Almost 300,000 remain temporarily without power
In the northwestern region of Volyn, which borders Poland, a drone strike on a food-processing facility killed one person and wounded eight others, according to Governor Roman Romaniuk. He said 370,000 people were temporarily without power in the morning, although 100,000 of them got supply back later on.
The blackout could last for at least 24 hours in Volyn's regional capital, Lutsk, Mayor Andriy Razumovskyi said on Facebook.
Romaniuk said that drone attacks continued throughout the day, striking a customs terminal and torching about 10 trucks in the town of Kovel, which sits on a major trunk road from Kyiv to Poland.
Other attacks hit at least two shopping centers, one in the northern city of Sumy, which sits close to the front line, and one in the neighboring region of Rivne, officials said, the latest in a spate of Russian assaults on malls and markets.
Pictures from emergency services in Sumy showed blood spattered across the floor and shots of the center's damaged entrance.
Seven people were wounded by drones that hit a major shopping center and other sites in Rivne, regional governor Oleksandr Koval said.
Ukraine's energy ministry said large parts of the city of Rivne and the surrounding area were without power after attacks on energy infrastructure there.
Russia, US to announce new joint initiatives beyond diesel deal
Russia and the United States will soon announce new joint initiatives beyond a recently agreed diesel deal, President Vladimir Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev said on Friday.
Dmitriev said the two countries were discussing joint data center projects, including facilities that could use electricity generated by Russian nuclear power plants.
Dmitriev said that the projects would be launched before the end of what Moscow calls its "special military operation" in Ukraine.
Following a report in the Financial Times that the US had proposed European countries transfer some frozen Russian assets to a vehicle overseen by Washington to try to revive stalled peace talks, Zelensky said that Ukraine could not risk any deal being struck to return the assets to Moscow.
Ukrainians struggling with a fifth year of Russian attacks on their power grid and other civilian infrastructure have said they are appalled by Trump's decision to open the US market for Russian diesel. They have also condemned his attempts to blame fuel shortages caused by the Iran war on Kyiv's military strikes on Russian refineries.

articles.title: Trump-Zelenskiy rift threatens vital support for Kyiv
articles.body:
Trump-Zelenskiy rift threatens vital support for Kyiv
WASHINGTON/KYIV, Oct 17 - From US threats to cut off intelligence support for Ukraine to a diesel deal that could help Russia fund its war, it has been a bad week for ties between Kyiv and its most important ally, Washington.
Frustrated by high energy costs he blames partly on Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, US President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. A disruption of US-provided satellite internet services raised fears that Ukraine could be vulnerable as it prepares for another winter of Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure.
Zelenskiy responded to Trump's barbs with an unusually sharp series of public criticisms of Trump, suggesting the US was now favoring Russia. He said Ukraine would defy Trump's demand to stop striking Russian energy targets, citing Russia's continued attacks.
The widening rift has sparked concerns that Trump and Zelenskiy's tumultuous relationship could lead to even worse outcomes for Kyiv. Trump could yet restrict the supply of weapons to Ukraine, follow through on threats to stop sharing battlefield intelligence, or strike more economic deals with Moscow.
Despite Zelenskiy's remarks, Kyiv wants to continue dialogue with Trump's envoys, his friend Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, two Ukrainian officials familiar with the talks said, speaking on the condition of anonymity.
Denys Sienik, chargé d'affaires at Ukraine's embassy in Washington, told Newsmax on Friday that Ukraine was grateful to Trump and his team for their efforts to end the war and said Ukraine was willing to engage in talks with Russia.
Trump told reporters on Friday he would continue to deal with both Zelenskiy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. “I want that war to end,” he said.
'MISSED OPPORTUNITY': FORMER US OFFICIAL
Daniel Fried, the senior State Department official on Europe from 2005 to 2009, said it was unclear whether Washington was making a lasting shift away from Ukraine, but the fallout was damaging prospects for an end to the war that began with Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion.
"It's not only a missed opportunity, it causes genuine suffering in Ukraine and encourages Putin to continue the war, so it's not cost-free," said Fried, now at the Washington-based Atlantic Council think tank.
Trump's relationship with Zelenskiy has long been uneasy. Trump and US Vice President JD Vance publicly upbraided Zelenskiy during an Oval Office meeting in February 2025. Washington has paused or slowed military assistance to Ukraine under Trump, while allowing European allies to purchase US weapons for Kyiv.
The relationship had steadied until Ukraine's strikes this year on energy sites in Russia began contributing to rising fuel prices. High gasoline and diesel prices are a political headache for Trump ahead of November's midterm elections, in which his Republican Party could lose its majorities in the US Congress, according to analysts.
Experts say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the US-Israeli war with Iran, which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz.
Frustrated by Zelenskiy, however, Trump turned to Russia to increase fuel supply and contain prices, according to a person familiar with the internal debate, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Trump said on October 9 he had reached a deal with Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel.
HIGH STAKES FOR UKRAINE
For Kyiv, the stakes are high and immediate. Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukraine had received no warning from Western partners before a deadly Russian attack on the capital.
Without US intelligence, Ukraine could face greater difficulty detecting and countering Russian missile and drone attacks, particularly against energy infrastructure that Moscow has repeatedly targeted during previous winters.
Trump has said the US is still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. But Zelenskiy told NPR that US officials had warned Ukrainian commanders intelligence could be reduced or cut off.
Ukraine's Starshield system, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink service, was disrupted after what two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter said was an order originating from the White House, Reuters reported on Thursday.
The service has been partially restored, but the episode highlighted the vulnerability created by Ukraine's dependence on technology controlled by US companies and subject to decisions by the Trump administration.
That dependence gives Trump potential leverage as he pushes Kyiv toward negotiations with Moscow.
Trump may face resistance if congressional Republicans see his approach as weakening Ukraine while benefiting Russia. Ukraine retains support among Trump's fellow Republicans, some of whom argue that Washington should not pressure Kyiv into accepting a settlement on terms favorable to Moscow.
Zelenskiy's tough responses to Trump were risky, but he may be counting on a power shift on Capitol Hill after the midterm elections to make it harder for Trump to ease sanctions on Russia and further reduce military assistance to Kyiv, said Brett Bruen, a former foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration and head of the Global Situation Room consultancy.
“Zelenskiy knows who he’s dealing with,” he said. “Trump’s threats don’t have the same kind of effect as they did when JD Vance tried to shame him in the Oval Office.” REUTERS

articles.title: Trump Halts Sweeping Russia Sanctions, Citing US National Interest
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump signed an executive order Friday, Oct. 16, suspending sweeping sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia just two days before they were due to take effect. Trump cited US national interests despite growing concerns that easing economic pressure on Moscow could help finance its war against Ukraine.
The executive order published by the White House waives major provisions of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which Trump signed into law on Sept. 18.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The suspended measures include additional 500% tariffs on Russian imports and 100% duties targeting the five largest buyers of Russian oil and natural gas, as well as countries facilitating Moscow’s sanctions evasion.
The restrictions were scheduled to take effect Sunday, Oct. 18, under legislation designed to cut the energy revenues sustaining Russia’s invasion.
“As described further in section 4 of this order, I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” Trump wrote.
The decision follows his controversial diesel agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin, which eased restrictions on Russian fuel exports amid rising global energy prices.
It also comes as relations between Washington and Kyiv have deteriorated, with President Volodymyr Zelensky warning that allowing Russia to earn more from energy sales could strengthen Putin’s ability to continue the war.
Zelensky: Starlink Still Not Fully Restored, Disrupting Drone Defense and Frontline Supplies
Trump suspends 500% tariffs and penalties on Russian oil buyers
Under the Graham Act, Congress authorized extensive economic measures against Russia’s energy and defense industries, financial institutions, senior officials and networks helping Moscow circumvent Western sanctions.
The legislation also provided for steep tariffs against countries continuing to purchase Russian energy, extending the financial consequences of Moscow’s invasion to its major trading partners.
Trump’s order sets out three major tariff categories:
- An additional 500% duty on goods imported from Russia.
- A 100% duty on imports from the five largest buyers making new purchases of Russian oil or natural gas beginning Oct. 18.
- A 100% duty on goods from the five leading countries facilitating Russian oil sanctions evasion.
However, the order simultaneously waives those duties, preventing their immediate application.
The decision shields major Russian energy customers, potentially including China and India, from new US trade penalties as long as the waiver remains in effect.
The measures also targeted Russia’s so-called shadow fleet – tankers used to transport Russian oil despite Western efforts to restrict Moscow’s energy exports.
Trump’s order suspends specified new sanctions provisions but does not remove restrictions already imposed under separate executive authorities.
Trump invokes national interest exemption
The president relied on Section 115 of the Graham Act, which allows sanctions, restrictions and tariffs to be waived if the administration certifies that doing so serves US national interests.
“I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States,” Trump stated.
The legislation also requires a report explaining the basis for that determination.
The executive order confirms that the certification and accompanying report were submitted to Congress, but does not publicly provide a detailed explanation of why suspending the additional penalties would serve US interests.
The waivers will remain in effect until Trump or designated administration officials determine that further action is appropriate.
The order directs the US Trade Representative, working with the State, Treasury and Energy departments, to continue monitoring Russian energy purchases and sanctions evasion.
Although the administration retains authority to reconsider the waivers, no timetable for restoring the measures was announced.
Bipartisan backlash over sanctions relief
Trump’s decision follows mounting criticism from lawmakers in both parties over the administration’s earlier agreement to ease restrictions on Russian diesel.
In a bipartisan letter to the administration, senators warned that allowing Russian energy exports could provide Moscow with additional revenue to finance military operations against Ukraine.
The criticism has extended beyond Democrats to Republicans who supported stronger economic pressure on Putin.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina has questioned the administration’s approach to the Russia diesel agreement and its implications for legislation championed by the late Lindsey Graham.
Democratic lawmakers have also challenged Trump’s decision to suspend sanctions Congress approved.
Representative Don Beyer accused the president of yielding to Putin, while Senator Elizabeth Warren criticized the administration for undermining congressional efforts to pressure Russia.
The dispute raises broader questions about the effectiveness of sanctions legislation when its implementation depends on presidential discretion.
Although the Graham Act remains law, its national interest waiver gives the administration substantial authority to prevent the new restrictions from taking effect.
Diesel deal with Putin precedes broader sanctions reversal
The decision comes one week after Trump agreed to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports in exchange for additional fuel supplies intended to ease pressure on international energy markets.
The agreement was presented by Washington as a response to rising fuel prices, which have been affected by the ongoing US-Israeli war against Iran and disruptions to global energy supplies.
Under the arrangement, Russia agreed to release hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel into international markets.
The White House has defended the cooperation as necessary to stabilize prices for American consumers and businesses.
However, critics argue that increasing Russian energy sales could replenish Moscow’s revenues at a time when Western sanctions are intended to limit its ability to sustain the invasion of Ukraine.
Kyiv condemns sanctions relief as Russia continues attacks
President Volodymyr Zelensky has criticized Washington’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian energy, warning that additional revenues could strengthen Moscow’s ability to finance its invasion.
He called the diesel arrangement a “weak decision” and insisted that Russia should face increased economic pressure rather than concessions.
The dispute has coincided with Trump’s criticism of Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil refineries.
Trump described Kyiv’s renewed attacks as a “disgrace,” arguing that they were contributing to higher global energy prices.
Zelensky has defended Ukraine’s efforts to weaken Russian oil infrastructure, which generates revenue supporting Moscow’s military operations.
Ukraine has also accused Russia of continuing to target Ukrainian energy facilities despite discussions about a possible mutual halt to attacks on energy infrastructure.
During Friday’s EU summit in Brussels, European Council President António Costa rejected the idea of easing pressure on Moscow.
“This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions,” Costa said.
“Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure.”

articles.title: Major Russian Strike on Vinnytsia Region Injures 6
articles.body:
Six people were injured and critical infrastructure was damaged during one of the largest Russian aerial assaults on Vinnytsia region since the start of the full-scale war, regional authorities reported on Saturday, Oct. 17.
Head of the Vinnytsia Regional Military Administration Nataliia Zabolotna confirmed on Facebook that Ukrainian air defense units intercepted 24 adversary strike drones over the region during the overnight engagement.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Despite defensive interceptions, incoming munitions struck civilian targets and vital infrastructure facilities across the province, leaving six people wounded.
“We have damage to civilian and critical infrastructure. Six people were injured,” Zabolotna said.
“One person is in intensive care in serious but stable condition. Three people are in moderate condition, and two others sustained minor injuries. All are receiving necessary medical treatment.”
Emergency utility repairs
Following the strikes, utility repair crews and electrical dispatchers enacted emergency operational protocols to restore disconnected municipal life-support systems.
Zabolotna reported that critical infrastructure sites across the impacted districts were transferred onto backup emergency generators to sustain baseline services while repair teams worked to restore municipal electricity and potable water supply.
Regional authorities appealed directly to residents across Vinnytsia region to conserve electricity and avoid overloading the vulnerable power grid as reconnection efforts progress.

“We urge residents of the region to switch on electrical appliances gradually and alternately as power is restored to prevent artificial overloads on the energy system,” Zabolotna stated.

articles.title: AI has enhanced Iran’s intelligence and targeting capabilities: Taeb
articles.body:
AI has enhanced Iran’s intelligence and targeting capabilities: Taeb
TEHRAN— Hossein Taeb, head of Iran’s Basij Organization, says the use of artificial intelligence in defense and intelligence operations has improved the accuracy of target identification and precision strikes, highlighting the technology’s growing role in Iran’s military capabilities.
Speaking on Thursday at the first Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity Conference in the southeastern city of Kerman, Taeb said AI had strengthened intelligence gathering and target assessment, adding that its applications had extended to the naval and aerospace divisions of Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) and other branches of the armed forces.
Taeb also discussed 'the objectives of the US-Israeli war against Iran,' arguing that attacks on military commanders, scientists and air-defense systems were intended to weaken the country’s defenses and undermine the scientific foundations of its development.
Protecting Iran’s scientific capabilities
Referring to the 12-day war, Taeb said the simultaneous targeting of military commanders and scientists was part of a strategy to weaken Iran’s security infrastructure and damage the scientific capabilities underpinning its technological progress.
He said the campaign against Iranian scientists had failed to eliminate the country’s nuclear expertise. According to Taeb, the scope of attacks expanded during the 40-day war, extending to other scientific fields and claiming the lives of researchers.
Taeb argued that the objective of such attacks went beyond military damage, encompassing efforts to undermine public security and weaken the country’s capacity for scientific and technological advancement.
"Targeting one scientist would not halt the country’s progress, as more specialists would emerge to continue the work," he said.
AI and the changing landscape of military operations
Taeb described investment in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity as a strategic decision for Iran’s future, calling for these priorities to be translated into practical action by government institutions, policymakers and leading experts.
He said AI had already produced tangible results in the defense sector by improving intelligence assessment and the accuracy of target identification.
He further said AI-assisted systems had improved the detection of military vessels operating near the Strait of Hormuz and helped increase missile accuracy. Taeb argued that these capabilities had affected US military calculations and contributed to the relocation of American naval vessels farther from the area.
His remarks underscore the growing importance of AI-enabled intelligence, surveillance and targeting systems in contemporary military operations. Such technologies can help process large volumes of information, identify patterns and support faster operational decisions, although their effectiveness depends on data quality, system reliability and human oversight.
Taeb highlights disparity in military spending
Taeb also contrasted Iran’s defense resources with the much larger military budgets of the United States and Israel. He cited figures for US military spending and additional wartime funding requests, and said Israel had received $22 billion in additional US assistance for the conflict.
Despite Iran’s limited defense resources in foreign-currency terms, Taeb said the country had been able to withstand the military campaign. He argued that a comparable emphasis on scientific capability, technological innovation and strategic planning was necessary to sustain progress in the fields of AI and cybersecurity.
He called for artificial intelligence and cybersecurity to move beyond isolated technological initiatives and become part of a coordinated national strategy involving public institutions and the country’s scientific community.
The conference’s focus on young technology specialists, Taeb said, reflected Iran’s intention to expand its pool of skilled researchers and developers. In his view, strengthening domestic expertise in emerging technologies is essential not only to defense preparedness but also to the country’s broader scientific and technological development.

articles.title: Russia wants blackout in Ukraine as winter comes — Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukraine: Zelenskyy urges allies to pressure Russia as energy sites hit
October 17, 2026
Russia is stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in a bid to cut electricity and heating in the country as winter approaches, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday.
His remarks come as Moscow intensifies its attacks on civilian targets in the capital, Kyiv, and elsewhere, with key observers saying its objective is to render the country virtually unlivable.
What did Zelenskyy say?
In a post on social media platform X, Zelenskyy said Russia had just carried out one of its biggest attacks on Ukraine's energy sector since it began its full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.
"More than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities were targeted across different regions of Ukraine," he wrote.
"Restoration work is ongoing, with all necessary services and all available resources of Ukrainian energy companies involved," he added.
Zelenskyy said that Russia was planning to leave Ukrainian citizens in the cold this winter.
"Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine — right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating," he wrote, calling on allies to put pressure on Moscow to stop this happening.
He said Russia had "expanded its campaign against the energy system" and was trying "to stretch Ukraine's reserves and repair capacity as thinly as possible." 
Russia claims multiple infrastructure attacks
The Russian Defense Ministry, for its part, said on Saturday that its forces had attacked several infrastructure targets in Ukraine overnight.
Among those named was an electricity substation in the northwestern city of Zhytomyr.
However, it also said Ukraine's largest steelworks, in the city of Kryvyi Rih, had been hit, saying the facility supplied steel products to the Ukrainian military-industrial complex.
It said another steel plant in Zaporizhzhia, a city near the front line, had also been struck.
Ukrainian authorities have also said that one person — an ambulance driver — was killed and 19 others injured, including a child, in a Russian airstrike on Kherson in southern Ukraine.
Russian state news agency TASS has also reported the death of one woman as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes in Russia's Belgorod region that also injured a man.
Trump's sanctions waiver a boost for Putin: Zelenskyy
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy also reacted to US President Donald Trump's decision to waive a package of new sanctions on Moscow, saying the move would only encourage Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
"A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking," Zelenskyy said.
On Friday, Trump signed an executive order that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia's energy revenues, two days before they were due to take effect.
The waiver has been hailed by a Russian presidential envoy as a "historic moment."
"The Trump administration's suspension of the [Lindsey] Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev said on social media.
Dmitriev said the act, named for the late US senator who sponsored the bill, "would have caused "serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets."
Trump's move came as he increasingly criticizes Zelenskyy, fueling speculation that the US leader is siding with Moscow in the conflict.

articles.title: Year-old startup wins spot in U.S. Army interceptor fly-off
articles.body:
- Furientis was selected as one of four vendors for a U.S. Army fly-off at the end of fiscal 2027 for a second IFPC Inc 2 interceptor.
- The year-old startup recently won its first funded Pentagon contract, raised $25 million, and unveiled a CAML launcher with Rheinmetall at AUSA.
Furientis, a missile startup founded just last year, has been picked as one of four companies to fly interceptors in a U.S. Army shoot-off at the end of fiscal 2027, competing to supply a second missile for the service’s Indirect Fire Protection Capability Increment 2 air defense system.
Co-founder and CEO Brody Franzen announced the selection, describing it as a downselect for a fly-off at the end of a fiscal year that closes on Sept. 30, 2027, without naming the other three companies chosen.
The Indirect Fire Protection Capability Increment 2, or IFPC Inc 2, is the U.S. Army’s mid-range air defense system for protecting bases and troops from cruise missiles, drones, rockets and artillery. Its truck-mounted Enduring Shield launcher, built by Leidos subsidiary Dynetics, now fires RTX’s AIM-9X Sidewinder, and the U.S. Army has spent the past few years looking for a second, more capable missile that can handle fast, low-flying cruise missiles and be built in larger numbers.
Lockheed Martin and a team of Boeing and Anduril are already competing in the formal second-interceptor program, which moved into its demonstration phase in September after Rafael’s U.S. subsidiary was not selected to continue. At the Association of the U.S. Army conference this week, Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano, the service’s portfolio acquisition executive for fires, said the U.S. Army would open a parallel path for companies that missed that first cut but kept investing in their own designs, inviting them to bring missiles to the range for a shoot-off in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, Breaking Defense reported, and Furientis’ selection appears to be part of that track.
Franzen and Aris Simsarian, both former engineers at Virgin Orbit and Castelion, founded Furientis in 2025 in the Los Angeles area to build interceptors designed for mass production from readily available parts. The company puts final assembly time at about 30 minutes and says it flight-tests prototypes roughly every two weeks instead of spending years on design before flying.
The startup came out of stealth in May with a $5 million pre-seed round, and on Oct. 6 it announced both a $25 million seed round led by Benchmark and its first funded government contract, a prototyping agreement with the U.S. Department of War for a 100-mile-range interceptor intended for homeland defense.
According to Franzen, the IFPC selection capped a busy two weeks in which Furientis flew its first horizontal flight test on a government range for the U.S. Army’s low-cost interceptor effort and, at AUSA, unveiled a containerized launcher developed with Rheinmetall for the U.S. Army’s Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher program.
He credited the U.S. Army’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Fires and its defensive fires team, led by Brig. Gen. Guy Yelverton, for opening the door to nontraditional vendors and giving them the resources to speed up development, and said Furientis is now hiring as it prepares its interceptor for the shoot-off due by the end of September 2027.

articles.title: Meeks Introduces Bill to Block Trump-Putin Diesel Deal
articles.body:
Representative Gregory Meeks, the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, introduced bipartisan legislation on Friday, Oct. 16, to prohibit the implementation of US President Donald Trump’s commercial diesel agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The draft measure, titled the “Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act,” aims to dismantle the administrative mechanisms facilitating Russian petroleum transactions, mandate sanctions against the Russian energy industry, and restrict federal financial backing for related enterprises, according to an official announcement by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

The legislative initiative explicitly prohibits the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) from investing in Russian energy projects, revokes all related general licenses issued by the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), and restricts executive agencies from issuing comparable sanctions exemptions in the future.
Meeks stated that the commercial agreement does not alleviate domestic economic pressures for American citizens, arguing that consumers are confronting elevated costs resulting from the administration’s military conflict with Iran.
Concurrently, the senior lawmaker warned that opening US and global markets to Russian diesel provides Moscow with critical hard-currency earnings that sustain military strikes against Ukrainian civilians.
Trump Denies Role in Slowing Ukraine’s Military Starlink
“At a time when the United States should be increasing pressure on the Kremlin, Donald Trump is cozying up to Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine,” Meeks said in a statement.
“This goes against everything the United States stands for. Congress must act. Every Member of Congress who claims to be outraged by this should join in passing this legislation.”
Bipartisan congressional pushback against energy accommodations
The introduction of Meeks’ bill accelerates a coordinated bipartisan effort on Capitol Hill to challenge the administration’s commercial accommodations toward Moscow.
The move follows legislative action initiated earlier in the week by Republican Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick and Don Bacon, who began drafting the “Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act” to establish a comprehensive statutory prohibition against importing Russian oil and refined hydrocarbons.
Lawmakers across both parties have criticized the administration for providing financial lifelines to the Kremlin’s defense sector while Ukrainian civilian and municipal energy networks face sustained long-range bombardments ahead of the winter heating season.
Under the framework announced by the White House following an Oct. 9 telephone call between Trump and Putin, Russia agreed to deliver commercial diesel fuel onto international markets through 2027. To facilitate the shipments, the US Treasury Department issued a general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
The commercial pivot drew immediate pushback from Kyiv, where President Volodymyr Zelensky characterized the timing of the arrangement as a “smokescreen” while Ukrainian and European negotiators were conducting multilateral peace discussions with US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami.
Executive suspension of Graham Act sanctions
The legislative drive arrives immediately following Trump’s signature on Friday, Oct. 16, of an executive order waiving major statutory sanctions and trade tariffs targeting the Russian Federation just 48 hours before they were scheduled to take effect.
The presidential waiver suspended key enforcement mechanisms enacted under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which Trump signed into law on Sept. 18.
The statute had established severe economic penalties designed to cut off revenues underwriting the Russian war effort, scheduled to enter into force on Sunday, Oct. 18.
Among the measures suspended by Trump’s order were an additional 500 percent tariff on all Russian-origin imports, alongside mandatory 100 percent duties targeting the five largest global purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas, such as China and India.
The waiver also suspended secondary tariffs on the five leading nations identified as facilitating the evasion of Russian petroleum sanctions, while halting prospective enforcement actions against Moscow’s maritime “shadow fleet” of tankers.
In the executive order, Trump asserted that waiving the Graham Act’s trade restrictions and duties aligned with US national interests, defending the step as necessary to manage global energy benchmarks.

Multiple US officials familiar with the matter told CBS that Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George’s risk analysis was included in the Pentagon's Global Force Management Allocation Plan in late December.
George was ousted by US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in April in the midst of the war with Iran.
According to CBS, George warned that both Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) battery and Patriot missile stockpiles would stay strategically low until at least 2030.
Anonymous US officials explained that George’s assessment stemmed from multiple factors, including the transfer of Patriot systems to Ukraine, munitions expended while defending Israel, and reduced defense industry production.
Officials told CBS that the US military does possess a significant stockpile of some offensive munitions, such as Joint Direct Attack Munitions (JDAM) and Small Diameter Bombs.
Over 50% of Patriot, THAAD interceptor stockpiles reportedly expended
Among the arms at critically low stock levels is the Patriot Advanced Capability-3 interceptor, a surface-to-air munition designed to destroy ballistic and cruise missiles mid-air.
Patriot PAC-3 orders have an average delivery time of over three years, CBS cited the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) as estimating in April. Defense contractors can take over four years to deliver a new shipment of THAAD interceptors.
CSIS estimated that prior to the Iran war, when George made his assessment, the US may have had around 2,300 Patriot interceptors. Between 1,050 and 1,430 interceptors, or up to 61% of prewar inventory, may have been expended during the war with Iran.
According to CSIS, pre-war THAAD stockpiles included about 355 interceptors. Between 190 and 290 of the munitions were allegedly used in the war, potentially using up 82% of the inventory.
Stockpiles could take four years to replenish, US official says
While American defense contractors have made moves to increase production of THAAD and Patriot interceptors, a US official told CBS that even if no more munitions were used, it could take until 2030 for the stockpiles to be fully replenished.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell denied the reports of munitions shortages in a statement to CBS, stating that the US has "everything required to strike at the time and place of the president's choosing."

articles.title: Why Ethiopia and Eritrea’s march to war demands global attention
articles.body:
The distant thunder of drones over Adigrat is not merely another African conflict. It is the sound of a continent’s most fragile peace shattering—and with it, the already slender prospects for stability across the Red Sea corridor that carries twelve per cent of global trade. Barely eight years after Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and President Isaias Afwerki embraced in Asmara, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate’s handshake now lies in ruins.
Eritrean troops have crossed into northern Tigray, advancing up to sixty kilometres into Ethiopian territory. Ethiopia has responded with multiple drone strikes targeting those forces, destroying lorries and ammunition, witnesses say, amid reports of civilian deaths. Both nations have severed diplomatic ties.
Ethiopia calls it an “all-out invasion.” Eritrea calls it an “unprovoked war of aggression.” The truth matters less than the trajectory: two of Africa’s most battle-hardened armies are edging toward a conflagration neither can afford, yet both seem convinced they cannot avoid.
The roots of this rupture are not mysterious. They are anchored in geography so cruel it functions as destiny. Ethiopia, home to 130 million people, is the world’s most populous landlocked nation. It depends on Djibouti for over 95 per cent of its maritime trade, paying between $1.5 and $2 billion annually in port fees—a haemorrhage equivalent to the cost of building a Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam every three years.
A nation that once commanded the Red Sea through the ancient port of Adulis now watches its commerce squeezed through a single corridor. This is not merely an economic inconvenience. It is a structural wound that successive Ethiopian leaders have described in existential terms.
Abiy’s response has been to demand sovereign maritime access—specifically, to the Eritrean port of Assab, barely sixty kilometres from the Ethiopian border. Eritrea, which won independence in 1993 after a thirty-year liberation struggle, views this as nothing less than a threat to its territorial integrity and the very meaning of its statehood. Asmara’s information minister has accused Ethiopia of openly working to bring about regime change by sheltering and supporting armed opposition groups. The result is a security dilemma of terrifying symmetry: each side’s defensive measures confirm the other’s worst fears.
Into this vacuum have stepped external powers with interests that have little to do with Ethiopian or Eritrean welfare. Israel has publicly endorsed Ethiopia’s Red Sea ambitions, with its ambassador describing support for the effort as “clear Israeli policy.”
The strategic logic is cold: a strong, allied Ethiopia provides a non-Arab anchor in a region where Israel seeks to counter Iranian and Houthi influence, and where its recognition of Somaliland has already signalled a willingness to redraw regional alignments. The United Arab Emirates, Ethiopia’s largest investor and a quiet supplier of military technology, forms the other pillar of this de facto axis.
The United States, by contrast, has intervened with uncharacteristic directness. On 14 October, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Abiy that “the region cannot tolerate more conflict,” demanding respect for sovereignty and an immediate halt to cross-border incursions. Washington has even lifted certain sanctions on Eritrea—a pragmatic pivot driven not by any moral reassessment but by the urgent need to secure Red Sea shipping lanes against Houthi attacks. This is containment dressed as diplomacy, and it carries an uncomfortable implication: accountability for Eritrea’s role in the Tigray war has been quietly subordinated to maritime security.
The regional picture is equally troubling. Egypt and Sudan have aligned themselves with Eritrea, driven by their own existential anxieties over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Cairo views the dam as a threat to its 97 per cent dependence on the Nile. Addis Ababa views it as a sovereign right.
The result is a “river-versus-sea” confrontation in which the Nile and the Red Sea have become inseparable theatres of competition. Ethiopia’s army chief has openly accused Egypt and Sudan of backing the very rebels now fighting federal forces.
The human cost of this geopolitical chess game is already being paid. The 2020–2022 Tigray war killed an estimated 600,000 people. A renewed interstate conflict—this time involving heavy drone strikes, conventional armies, and the potential spillover onto Eritrea’s Red Sea coast—would create a humanitarian catastrophe of a different magnitude entirely. Millions of Ethiopians already face severe food insecurity.
The fragile Pretoria Agreement that ended the Tigray war has dissolved into renewed fighting across Amhara and Afar, with former allies now united in an armed alliance against the federal government. Ethiopia cannot fight a civil war and an interstate war simultaneously without fracturing.
Yet the most disturbing truth is that neither Washington’s pressure nor the African Union’s exhortations have altered the trajectory. The AU, headquartered in Addis Ababa, is structurally compromised—it cannot credibly mediate a conflict involving its host nation.
The Gulf states possess the financial leverage to broker a settlement, but the UAE’s deep ties to Ethiopia and Saudi Arabia’s alignment with Egypt make a unified mediation unlikely. The window for diplomacy is closing, and it is closing fast.
What is required is not another communiqué. It is a recognition that Ethiopia’s landlocked status is not a moral failing to be corrected by force, but a structural reality that demands a structural solution. The path forward lies in negotiated maritime access frameworks, joint port management arrangements, and regional economic integration that makes war materially irrational.
Ethiopia’s accession to the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System in October 2026 offered a glimpse of what patient, institutional cooperation could achieve. That glimpse is now being extinguished by the roar of drones.
The international community must act with a clarity that matches the urgency. The United States, the Gulf states, and the African Union must coordinate a single, unambiguous message: there is no military solution. But pressure alone is insufficient. The world’s strategic powers must offer Ethiopia a credible economic alternative—guaranteed, legally binding access to Red Sea ports under international law, backed by investment and infrastructure. Eritrea, for its part, must be assured that its sovereignty is not a bargaining chip.
The Horn of Africa has burned before. The world watched then, and the world did too little. It must not watch again. The drones over Adigrat are not a warning. They are a countdown.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

articles.title: U.S. Air Force adds drone-mimicking firm to adversary pool
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force awarded KestrelX, A2G International and Fleet Adversary Support and Training places on a $5.4 billion adversary air and close air support contract.
- Work runs across the continental United States through Oct. 8, 2029, with only $3,000 obligated at award and funding to follow through task orders.
The U.S. Air Force has added three small companies to a contract worth up to $5.4 billion for privately flown “Red Air” adversary aircraft and close air support training, including a firm that flies small planes made to mimic enemy drones and cruise missiles.
KestrelX of Driggs, Idaho, A2G International of Melbourne, Florida, and Fleet Adversary Support and Training of St. Augustine, Florida, each received a place on the indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract for the Combat Air Force Contracted Air Support program, the U.S. Department of War said. The Air Combat Command Acquisition Management and Integration Center at Langley Air Force Base, Virginia, awarded the deals on Oct. 15 after a competition in which three offers were received. Only $3,000 was obligated at signing, with money to flow later through individual task orders.
Under the program, private companies supply aircraft and pilots that play the enemy, or Red Air, against U.S. fighter crews in training, and fly close air support sorties so joint terminal attack controllers on the ground can practice calling in airstrikes. Work will take place across the continental United States through Oct. 8, 2029.
The new awards carry the same $5.4 billion ceiling and a nearly identical end date as the second Combat Air Force Contracted Air Support contract, which the U.S. Air Force awarded in September 2024 to eight established adversary air companies, including Airborne Tactical Advantage Company, Draken International, Top Aces and Tactical Air Support. Those firms compete with one another for task orders under the vehicle, and the original version, awarded in 2019, had a $6.4 billion ceiling.
KestrelX brings a different kind of aircraft to that pool. The company, founded by former U.S. Navy fighter and test pilot Don Moseley, flies small jets and light propeller planes modified to replicate drones and cruise missiles, and it has played those threats in exercises such as Northern Strike in Michigan. Last month, the U.S. Navy hired KestrelX under a contract worth up to $9.99 million to supply low-observable target aircraft and engineering support for training exercises.
A2G International describes itself as an operator of manned and unmanned aircraft that provides airborne intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance services to U.S. and foreign government customers.
Contracted Red Air grew as the U.S. Air Force ran short of its own aggressor aircraft and did not want to tie up front-line fighters, particularly F-35s, playing the enemy in training. A 2021 Government Accountability Office report found that the U.S. Air Force planned for adversary air contracts to serve as a bridge, with their use expected to phase out around 2030 as the service builds up its own aggressor squadrons and explores new crewed and uncrewed adversary aircraft.
Each of the three new companies will now be able to compete for task orders under the contract through October 2029.

articles.title: Independent Scotland would leave UK forces their kit
articles.body:
EXCLUSIVE – An independent Scotland would, the Scottish National Party believe, have a legitimate claim on its proportionate share of British military equipment but would decline to exercise it if taking the kit caused serious problems for what remained of the United Kingdom, the SNP Westminster leader told me when I sat down with him to chat all things defence.
Dave Doogan, the member for Angus and Perthshire Glens, said the ownership position is clear even if the practical answer is not: “It’s important to remember that we own the assets, all of them proportionately, at the disposal of the UK defence forces, and so we’ve got a call on them. But why would we make problems for the UK by taking our share?”
He set that against the state of the British inventory, where he argues the margin for giving anything away has long since gone: “You know as well as I do that there is very little redundancy in any platform in the United Kingdom. You know, just look at what they were trying to do to get a functioning Type 45 out to the Mediterranean recently. If we think that there are squadrons of Typhoons up and down these islands ready to go at a moment’s notice, that’s not how it is.”
On that basis he ruled out pressing a claim that damaged the rest of the UK, telling me “So if we were to claim our share of eight per cent or whatever of UK assets, and that caused major difficulties for the UK, well, we just wouldn’t do it because it’s not intelligent.”
Division of assets has been one of the hardest parts of the independence argument to pin down since 2014, when the Scottish Government’s white paper assumed Scotland would inherit a share of equipment and the then British government declined to negotiate before a vote. The eight per cent figure Doogan uses reflects Scotland’s rough share of the British population, which was the basis the 2014 prospectus worked from.
Indeed, his point about redundancy lands on a fleet that has been audited repeatedly on exactly that question. The Royal Navy’s six Type 45 destroyers have spent much of the past decade affected by the propulsion problems now addressed through the Power Improvement Project.
Doogan expects the negotiation to be conducted without rancour once the constitutional question is settled, and said the hostility between the two governments is a product of the constitutional argument itself: “That’s the world that we will actually enter after independence. It will be about constructive and mature discussion about here’s where we were, here’s where we are, where do we want to get to, and how do we do that in the best interests of an independent Scotland and the rest of the UK. Because this enmity that exists just now is a function of trying to keep the UK together. Once Scotland’s out of the UK, that enmity has no purpose anymore, and we’ll work together like grown-up and respectful states.”
He argued that cooperation would follow from self-interest on both sides, and that the rest of the UK would deal with Scotland as it deals with everywhere else it once governed: “Let’s not pretend for one minute that the United Kingdom, once all the heat has gone out of an independence debate and Scotland has chosen to be independent, the rest of the UK will cooperate with Scotland just in the same way it cooperates with every other entity and jurisdiction that used to be governed from London. It’s entirely predictable, because it’s to England’s and the rest of the UK’s self interest to cooperate with Scotland, and it’s in Scotland’s interest to cooperate with the rest of the UK.”
The loss of jurisdiction over the northern half of the island would present a problem, he accepted, and one he does not expect to be handled adversarially: “If the SNP or I have got anything to do with that, that won’t be a challenge because we’ll approach it in a cooperative way. How we do that is up for discussion. A brand new independent Scotland would not want to be undefended, but the rest of the UK would not wish a brand new independent Scotland to be undefended either.”
On the deterrent, Doogan said an independent Scotland would have no further locus once the system left Scottish waters, and would take no view on what Westminster did with it afterwards: “It’s not a Scottish asset or system, it’s a UK asset or system. And so what they choose to do with it, where they choose to berth it, whether they choose to sustain and renew it going forward into the future, that’s entirely up to the rest of the UK. Scotland will have no role in that. We’ll respect their sovereignty and their freedom of decision, and they’ll respect ours.”
The kit Scotland would be declining to take is itself under question in his view, and he turned to the surface fleet while discussing the Type 32 frigate, the conceptual class folded into the Future Cruiser Combat Vessel programme without a commitment on where it would be built: “If I’m being honest and being fair, there is now a serious question mark about how many big grey ships you put on the surface of the sea, and how expensive and challenging it is to defend these assets now.”
He went on to set out the arithmetic that worries him, with the air defence destroyers tied to the carriers and the frigates left to look after themselves: “I don’t doubt the capabilities of Type 45, old as it is. It’s still a very potent warship, assuming it’s actually able to move itself, which is not guaranteed with 45. But it’s going to be busy defending two hulking great aircraft carriers, and so 31 and 26 are going to have to do a job defending themselves. That looks increasingly expensive against a volley, literally volley, of inexpensive, very hard to intercept drones.”
That point about escorts protecting themselves runs into an arithmetic problem the whole alliance is grappling with, because a Sea Ceptor round costs a great deal more than the one-way attack drones now being fired in salvoes at ships in the Red Sea and the Black Sea, and the Royal Navy has been working through directed energy and gun-based answers, including DragonFire, for exactly that reason. The Type 45s carry Sea Viper and Aster for area air defence, the capability the carriers depend on, and the fleet has six of them.
Doogan was also blunt about the policy architecture that was supposed to keep the yards busy into the next decade, recalling the ministerial appointments and slogans that have come and gone during his time in the Commons: “I’ve only been in Parliament seven years, and I remember when there was a shipbuilding czar. It was actually Ben Wallace, the Secretary of State for Defence. Not heard much about a shipbuilding czar recently. I remember when it was all about a shipbuilding pipeline. It was an end to boom and bust was what it was going to be. Well, it just goes to show you that those words are easy. What’s difficult is putting the resource in place to make sure that that happens.”
Doogan accepted that competing orders internationally is the straightforward part of the problem, “An anti-boom and bust and an actual pipeline of work, especially when you’re building grey ships, you have to compete it. Unfortunately, you have to compete it internationally. That’s easy. Let’s have, like, a no-brainer. What’s harder is to find the budget.”
On the wider state of conventional forces, he described a force he believes is being hollowed out around the edges, and listed what he sees when he looks at it: “If our soldiers were delighted, if our airmen felt that they had a purpose and that they could get more than a couple of flying hours a month, if our combat aircraft were properly armed, if we stopped buying systems that are fitted for but not with, because we can’t afford to put the missiles in the launch tubes that these systems have, if we weren’t practising launching artillery with two shells a day or a session, because there isn’t enough.”
He acknowledged where some of the ammunition has gone, while arguing that the replenishment should have followed: “Some of that, of course, is because we’ve sent so much artillery to Ukraine. But shells aren’t complex. We should be replenishing them, and it’s unfortunate that that money is just not there.”
Doogan put a figure on the shortfall he believes the Chancellor is facing, and drew a line around the nuclear enterprise while doing it: “You’ll need to find an extra fifteen to twenty billion for defence, and that’s going to be a real challenge. And that’s fifteen, twenty billion for the whole of defence outside the nuclear enterprise.”
The Type 32 was announced by Boris Johnson in November 2020 as a fifth-generation class of general purpose frigates intended to follow Type 31, and it never progressed beyond concept before being absorbed into the Future Cruiser Combat Vessel work that is now running alongside the Type 83 destroyer replacement for Type 45. Rosyth has gone from assembling the Queen Elizabeth class carriers to building the five Type 31 frigates in the Venturer Building, and the sustainability of that drumbeat after the Type 31 order runs out has been a persistent concern in Fife.
Talking about British kit and Scottish yards at this length is itself a change, and Doogan has been pushing his own party in that direction for years against a habit he describes as widespread across Scotland: “Within the SNP more generally, there is a kind of tacit reluctance to engage with defence issues, for a lot of people in Scotland, not just in the SNP. Defence in Scotland begins and ends with the deterrent. There’s an awful lot more to defence in Scotland than the deterrent. But conventional defence is really important, and I’ve worked really hard to try and get that up the SNP’s agenda.”
He called the shift a positive thing and cited the First Minister’s recent visit to Babcock at Rosyth, along with a run of further visits by SNP elected members to defence establishments in Scotland, both completed and upcoming. He traced the argument back to the party’s NATO policy and what he thinks it obliges a government to do: “SNP policy is to be part of NATO. If you want to be part of NATO, you have to accept that peace and security doesn’t land at your feet. And if you don’t ensure by your own words, deeds and resources that you can do everything you possibly can to secure your peace and security, well then you’re not much use as a government to your people, and you’re not much use to your allies as a partner in peace and security.”
He said the case lands with colleagues when it is put to them directly, and that it follows from something the party already accepts about the armed forces: “When you speak to people about it, that’s not a controversial view in the SNP, and I think that’s a good thing, and it’s a work in progress, and people I think are accepting of it because actually it’s an extrapolation of, if we hold our men and women in uniform in the highest of regard, then we must hold what they do in the highest of regard, and if we do that, then we have to accept that they need to be equipped, and that allows us to hold defence manufacturers in high regard too.”
Doogan spent his career in defence engineering, working on Ministry of Defence helicopters, before entering Parliament in 2019. Asked what he would say to a young person in Scotland weighing up a career in the sector, he was unequivocal: “Any young person looking at possibly taking a job in engineering, do it. And getting a job in engineering and defence, do it, because if for no other reason, in defence you’re operating to the highest of standards in the best of conditions often, and those skills are in huge demand globally and domestically. So it’s a very good employment opportunity.”
He had made a related point at an industry event the previous evening, taking issue with the way politicians talk about employment: “Politicians have a habit of just talking about jobs in abstract, as though all jobs are equal. All jobs are not equal. Engineering jobs are an extremely attractive career proposition, and defence engineering jobs in particular are an extremely attractive employment proposition. So anybody thinking about that, I would say go on ahead and do it, because the more people that repopulate our defence sector in Scotland, the better.”
The same session covered the sub-threshold threats facing Britain and Scotland, which he put in terms of the damage they do to ordinary economic life: “Talking about the range of sub-threshold grey zone threats that we face, which aren’t in themselves the end of the world, but are a serious impediment. See Jaguar Land Rover, serious impediment to our freedom and liberty and our economy and people’s jobs.”
Doogan’s comments come a day after the Scottish Government confirmed it will match the ten million pounds offered by the Ministry of Defence to establish two Defence Technical Excellence Colleges in Scotland, ending a wait of seven months since the offer was made in March. Alyn Smith, the Innovation Minister, wrote jointly with Economy Secretary Stephen Flynn to confirm the money, with sites to be allocated in the east and west of the country covering defence engineering, advanced manufacturing and maritime technology.
The sector Doogan wants repopulated employs a substantial number of people across Scotland. BAE Systems builds the Type 26 frigates at Govan and Scotstoun, Babcock assembles the Type 31 at Rosyth, Leonardo produces radar and electronic warfare equipment in Edinburgh, Thales builds optronics and missile systems at Govan, and Raytheon operates at Glenrothes. All of them compete for the same welders, electrical technicians and systems engineers, and all of them have warned about the pipeline.
The SNP’s position on defence has moved considerably over the past two years, with the Programme for Government committing to a responsible defence industrial growth programme, a formulation that keeps public money away from munitions while backing the wider sector. Doogan describes the shift inside his own party as unfinished work.

articles.title: Ousted US general warned before Iran war of missile defense shortages lasting until 2030: Report
articles.body:
Ousted US Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George warned months before the US-Israeli war against Iran that American missile defense stockpiles were critically low and could take until 2030 to recover, CBS News reported Thursday.
George raised the warning in late December, two months before the conflict began, according to US officials familiar with his assessment. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed him from his post in April as the war was underway.
The general’s assessment, included in the Pentagon’s fiscal 2027 force allocation planning, identified shortages of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors and Patriot missiles, with supplies expected to remain at strategically low levels until 2030.
The officials reportedly attributed the shortfall to weapons transfers to Ukraine, US military support for Israel, and limited defense industry production capacity.
The war with Iran has further strained supplies, according to the report. A Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimate found that US forces entered 2026 with approximately 2,300 Patriot interceptors and used between 1,050 and 1,430 during the conflict.
READ: US considering using ‘mother of all bombs’ against Iran: Report
The country’s prewar THAAD inventory stood at around 355 interceptors, of which an estimated 190 to 290 were expended.
Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and senior adviser at CSIS, told CBS News that these systems would be crucial in a potential conflict with China.
“Air defense — missile defense — that will be huge,” he said, explaining that a major confrontation with Beijing would demand substantial interceptor supplies.
Replenishing the stockpiles remains a lengthy process, the report said. The CSIS estimates that new THAAD interceptor contracts take over four years to fulfill, while Patriot PAC-3 orders take an average of 3 1/2 years.
The Pentagon rejected claims of a shortage. Chief spokesman Sean Parnell told CBS News: “Claims of U.S. munitions shortages are false.”
He added that Washington retains “everything required to strike at the time and place of the President’s choosing.”
