articles.title: Iran reaffirms Strait of Hormuz closure, says passage must be coordinated
articles.body:
Iran reaffirms Strait of Hormuz closure, says passage must be coordinated
TEHRAN — Iranian military officials have reiterated that the Strait of Hormuz remains closed to uncoordinated maritime traffic, linking any easing of restrictions to 'respect for Iran’s rights' and warning that continued US military presence in the region will deepen insecurity.
Rear Admiral Habibollah Sayyari, deputy coordinator of the Iranian Army, said on Thursday that any vessel seeking to transit the strategic waterway must coordinate its passage with the Iranian authorities who are in charge. His remarks came as Army Chief Commander Major General Amir Hatami and Army Spokesman Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia issued separate statements emphasizing Iran’s military readiness and its determination to maintain control over the security environment around the strait.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a ceremony honoring Army nurses, Sayyari argued that the impact of restrictions on maritime traffic was evident in international fuel markets.
“The Strait of Hormuz is closed. If it were open and oil were passing through it, gasoline prices in the United States would not have risen,” he said.
Sayyari outlined the deployment of Iran’s armed forces around the waterway, saying the naval forces of Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) maintained a firm presence to the west of the strait, while the Iranian Army operated to its east and extended its presence northward into the Sea of Oman.
He stressed that any passage through the waterway must be coordinated, warning that vessels attempting to transit without such coordination could face consequences.
Hatami links reopening to respect for Iran’s rights
Army Chief Commander Major General Amir Hatami has also made clear that, in Iran’s view, the future of the strait is directly linked to the treatment of the country and its rights.
Speaking at Imam Ali Officers’ University in Tehran on Thursday, Hatami said the Strait of Hormuz had been closed following the outbreak of the war and would remain closed until Iran’s rights were respected.
He attributed the conflict to a ‘fundamental miscalculation by Iran’s adversaries,’ who had underestimated the country’s military capabilities and assumed that it was in a weakened position.
According to Hatami, the Iranian Army and the IRGC responded from the earliest hours of the conflict with extensive strikes against hostile targets. He argued that the adversaries had failed to achieve their military and strategic objectives.
Rejecting US assertions that Iran’s military capabilities had been weakened, the Army chief pointed to continued missile and drone operations and the functioning of the country’s air-defense systems as evidence of its sustained operational capacity.
Hatami also said Iran had taken firm action against vessels that violated its regulations, leaving maritime traffic through the strait severely restricted.
He added that Iran’s armed forces had used the pause in hostilities to repair damage and strengthen their readiness. Iranian ground, naval, air-defense and missile units, he said, remained equipped and prepared to defend the country’s territorial integrity.
Hatami further warned that any attack on Iran’s infrastructure would prompt a response inflicting substantially greater damage on the infrastructure and interests of its adversaries, including Israel and those cooperating with it.
Army says US military presence fuels regional insecurity
In separate remarks on Friday, Army spokesman Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia said Iran was developing new operational plans that would force hostile US naval vessels to withdraw even farther from the country’s coastline.
Akraminia said Iran’s air-defense capabilities had advanced beyond their prewar and wartime levels, adding that Iranian air-defense units had intercepted several US drones in the country’s airspace in recent weeks. He also said US military vessels had been pushed to distances exceeding 500 kilometers from the coasts of the Persian Gulf.
The spokesman described the US military presence as a central source of insecurity in the region and called on regional countries and the international community to recognize ‘Washington’s role in fueling instability.’
“If America leaves the region, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen, and collective security will be established with the participation of the region’s countries, and the global economy will improve. If it doesn’t leave, we’ll expel it,” Akraminia said.
He added that Iranian forces had rehearsed advanced, coordinated and innovative military operations, while nationwide air-defense coverage had been significantly strengthened.
A strategic waterway with global economic consequences
The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most strategically important energy corridors, connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the wider Arabian Sea. A substantial share of global oil shipments and significant volumes of liquefied natural gas pass through the waterway, making disruptions a concern for energy-importing countries, shipping operators and financial markets.
Restrictions on traffic through the strait can raise shipping and insurance costs, disrupt energy supplies and add volatility to oil and fuel prices. The effects depend on the scale and duration of the disruption, the availability of alternative supplies and routes, and market expectations about the conflict.
Iran’s latest statements place the waterway at the center of its broader security position: Tehran says passage must be coordinated, its armed forces remain prepared, and any change in the current situation depends on respect for Iran’s rights and the future of foreign military deployments in the region.
The statements also underscore the competing approaches to security in the Persian Gulf. While Washington has emphasized maritime security and freedom of navigation, Iranian officials argue that lasting stability requires regional cooperation and an end to ‘destabilizing foreign military intervention.’
With energy markets and international shipping exposed to developments around the strait, any sustained change in maritime traffic is likely to have consequences well beyond West Asia. For Iran, however, the issue is not solely one of commercial passage: its military leadership has framed the waterway as a strategic lever tied to national security, sovereignty and the outcome of the wider confrontation.

articles.title: Heavy cost for US to return to confrontation with Iran
articles.body:
The experience of recent conflicts has demonstrated that possessing advanced weaponry and massive firepower does not necessarily equate to achieving strategic objectives. Factors such as depletion of military stockpiles, damage to military equipment, need to procure replacement ammunition, and Iran’s capacity to restore its defensive capabilities all serve to complicate the White House’s calculations regarding a potential re-engagement in military confrontation with powerful Iran.
In a report citing the financial and military costs of past US strikes against Iran, the British newspaper “The Times” highlights the significant strain this conflict has placed on Washington’s military resources. According to the report, US expenditures have exceeded $43 billion in this war, dozens of American aircraft have sustained damage, and the US stockpiles of interceptor missiles have come under pressure. Regardless of the final assessment of the conflict's military outcomes, these figures indicate that sustaining large-scale operations against Iran requires substantial financial and material resources, the resources that cannot be replaced or replenishment in the short term is impossible.
The significance of this issue becomes even greater when the direct costs of military operations are weighed alongside their strategic consequences. In military calculations, the number of attacks carried out or the volume of ammunition expended is not, in itself, the definitive measure of victory. What truly matters is the ratio between the costs incurred and the objectives intended to be achieved through those expenditures. If a military operation entails the extensive use of ammunition and damage to equipment, yet fails to eliminate the adversary’s capacity to continue their resistance, persisting with the same approach may simply lead to mounting costs with no guarantee that the desired outcome will ever be attained.
Erosion of Military Stockpiles: Washington’s Hidden Challenge
One of the most significant consequences of a military conflict is the strain placed on stockpiles of weapons and ammunition. The extensive use of interceptor missiles to counter threats from missiles and drones, particularly when attacks are sustained, can deplete ready-to-use stockpiles, thereby increasing the need for production and resupply. This issue is of particular importance to the United States. In addition to its military commitments in West Asia, Washington must also ensure its forces remain prepared to address potential crises in other parts of the world.
Replenishing arms stockpiles is not merely a matter of securing funding. The production of certain advanced systems and the ammunition they utilize requires complex supply chains, specialized raw materials, and specialized industrial capacity. However, even if new budget allocations are made, rapidly replacing expended stocks is not necessarily feasible. The higher the rate of ammunition consumption in a conflict, the greater pressure placed on production schedules, the prioritization of arms deliveries, and the allocation of resources toward other military missions.
Under such circumstances, Washington’s decision to launch a new round of strikes is not limited merely to an assessment of operational capability; rather, it must also account for the opportunity cost of expending munitions and the subsequent impact on US military readiness. In other words, every missile used in an operation must be evaluated within the context of the United States’ broader defense requirements.
Iran’s Capacity for Recovery and Difficulty of Achieving a Definitive Outcome
On the other side of this equation lies Iran’s capacity to maintain and restore its defensive capabilities. In a report, “The Times” notes that, despite military attacks and pressures, Iran has managed to recover a portion of its missile and drone capabilities. This is significant from the perspective of military calculations, as the effectiveness of an offensive operation depends, to a large extent, on the degree of its lasting impact on the adversary’s capabilities.
If military strikes fail to permanently dismantle a nation’s defensive capacity, inflicting damage at a specific point in time does not necessarily equate to eliminating that nation’s ability to continue its resistance. The potential to repair equipment, restore certain operational capabilities, and maintain the capacity to produce or deploy weaponry can alter the conflict’s equation over time. In such a scenario, the aggressor may be compelled to repeatedly expend further munitions and equipment to sustain military pressure—all while the ultimate outcome of this process remains uncertain. The strategic implication is clear: as long as the adversary retains the ability to continue resisting, one cannot conclude that their defensive capacity has been exhausted based solely on the volume of attacks carried out.
Why could a renewed attack be more costly?
The United States re-engaging in a confrontation with Iran could trigger a repeat of that same costly cycle. New operations would require ammunition, logistics equipment, fuel supplies, the movement of troops, and the protection of military bases and facilities. Should equipment sustain damage or the scope of the conflict expand, costs would rise accordingly. Furthermore, a prolonged crisis could impact energy markets and economic expectations, extending the repercussions well beyond the military battlefield.
On the other hand, the United States must also consider the possibility of a prolonged conflict and the need to remain prepared for unforeseen scenarios. Military operations might begin with limited objectives, but reciprocal responses and shifting conditions could expand their scope. Under such circumstances, the final cost will not necessarily align with initial estimates.
The fundamental question for the White House is whether the costs of a new confrontation would yield commensurate gains. If the objective is to durably weaken Iran’s defensive capabilities, the persistence of its missile and drone capacities could make achieving this goal more difficult. Furthermore, if the aim is to compel Tehran to accede to Washington’s demands, it remains to be seen whether military pressure would truly lead to such an outcome, or if it would merely generate additional costs.
The White House’s Strategic Calculus Test
A report by “The Times” once again draws attention to the gap between military superiority and the achievement of strategic outcomes. Possessing extensive military capabilities enables the infliction of damage, but it does not, in itself, guarantee that the adversary will cease resistance or that the aggressor’s political objectives will be realized. When assessing a conflict, one must simultaneously consider the costs incurred, the resilience of the parties involved, and the extent to which objectives have been achieved.
For Washington, returning to a confrontation with Iran—without regard for the lessons of past costs—means re-entering a path with a predetermined outcome. The strain on U.S. military stockpiles, combined with Iran’s ability to restore parts of its defensive capabilities, suggests that repeating such attacks will not necessarily shift the equation in favor of the aggressor.
Ultimately, the primary challenge for the United States is not merely the capacity to launch a new operation, but the ability to achieve a sustainable outcome at a manageable cost. If previous strikes failed to realize Washington’s intended objectives, any decision to follow the same path requires a clear answer to the question: what will be different this time? Absent such an answer, a renewed attack risks becoming less of a solution to the crisis and more the beginning of another phase of resource depletion and escalating strategic costs for the United States.
MNA

articles.title: The illusion of victory over Iran
articles.body:
The illusion of victory over Iran
In an article, Donya-e-Eqtesad discussed what it described as Washington’s illusion of victory over Iran. Citing international affairs analyst Farid Zakaria, the newspaper argued that military success does not necessarily produce political or strategic success.
The article notes that although the United States speaks of victory, it is still attempting to restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The main issue, according to the paper, is not only the strait itself or the military and economic costs involved, but the absence of a clear American objective. The Trump administration, it argues, has not clarified whether its goal is changing Iran’s behavior or changing the Iranian government. The article contends that Washington must choose between these approaches. If the goal is to alter Iranian policies, reopen the strait, limit the nuclear program, and curb Tehran’s regional activities, then the United States should pursue realistic goals through pressure and negotiation. If regime change is the actual objective, America must prepare for a costly conflict with consequences extending beyond the Middle East.
 
Kayhan: Violation equals punishment
Kayhan wrote that recent military developments in the Strait of Hormuz show, contrary to Donald Trump’s statements, that Iran is fully enforcing its authority over the strategic waterway. According to the newspaper, Iranian armed forces are taking action against vessels that violate Iranian regulations. During recent regional tensions, the Persian Gulf, particularly the Strait of Hormuz, has become both an active arena of confrontation and a demonstration of Iran’s military capabilities. The paper argues that Western plans to bypass the strait through alternative routes have failed. Investments in pipelines and southern transit corridors were intended to reduce reliance on Hormuz, but recent events allegedly demonstrated that Iran’s deterrent and operational reach extend beyond the strait itself. According to Kayhan, these developments prove that no secure alternative route can eliminate Iran’s leverage and that the waterway remains under Iranian authority.
Hamshahri: American warships, power projection or operational constraint?
Hamshahri examined reports that US naval forces are operating roughly 700 to 800 kilometers from the Strait of Hormuz. Quoting the commander of the IRGC Navy, the paper stated that an American aircraft carrier remains at that distance because of vulnerability concerns and has avoided entering areas within the reach of Iranian forces. The article notes that Washington has long used aircraft carriers as symbols of military power and tools of pressure. Military analysts, however, argue that effectiveness depends not only on the number of ships and weapons available but also on vulnerability to an opponent’s missiles and operational capabilities. According to the paper, the fleet’s distance from the strait raises questions about whether American claims regarding maritime security fully match operational realities.
Sobh-e-No: Hormuz is completely locked
Sobh-e-No argued that Iran’s policy in the Strait of Hormuz has entered a new and more assertive phase. According to the newspaper, movement through the waterway faces tighter restrictions while Iran is expanding measures designed to enforce new navigation rules. The article states that increased attacks on vessels accused of violations indicate that Iran’s approach has moved beyond warnings and statements into active implementation. In its view, the current situation represents more than a rise in maritime incidents. Rather, Tehran is using its geographical position, energy influence, and political leverage to increase pressure on Washington. The newspaper argues that a military option could trigger a broader regional conflict and drive oil prices sharply higher. On the other hand, continued restraint could allow Iran to strengthen its influence over global energy flows. The article concludes that negotiations remain the most practical route to reducing tensions.
Javan: War reaches the heart of the digital economy
In a commentary on the implications of regional tensions for artificial intelligence, Javan examined risks facing major technology investments in the Persian Gulf. The newspaper noted that hundreds of billions of dollars have been invested in AI projects and data centers that support ambitions to make the region a global technology hub. According to the report, rising military tensions have increased concerns about the security of critical digital infrastructure. As Persian Gulf economies become more dependent on cloud services, data centers, and advanced technologies, any expansion of conflict could threaten economic stability and technological development. The article argues that potential military actions affecting infrastructure linked to American technology companies create a new connection between warfare, deterrence, and economic security. It warns that the consequences could extend beyond the battlefield and influence future investment decisions across the region. Dr. Mohammad Reza Ghasemi, an adviser to the Iranian Parliament’s Artificial Intelligence faction, stated that a significant escalation of conflict could lead to widespread disruptions in international internet connectivity and serious interruptions to everyday life.

articles.title: Bill tabled in US Congress to block deal on Russian diesel fuel
articles.body:
Bill tabled in US Congress to block deal on Russian diesel fuel
Gregory Meeks, a Democrat and Ranking Member of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee, has introduced a bipartisan bill aimed at blocking the US-Russia deal on diesel fuel.
Source: the US House Foreign Affairs Committee's website
Details: The bill would prohibit the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) from investing in Russia's energy sector; revoke general licences issued by the US Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) and prohibit future licences; and require US President Donald Trump's administration to impose sanctions on Russia's energy sector.
The bill has 17 co-sponsors in the House of Representatives.
Quote from Meeks: "This deal won't lower costs for the American people, who are already paying for Trump's failed war of choice in Iran. It will hand Putin millions of dollars to continue slaughtering Ukrainian civilians with impunity."
"At a time when the United States should be increasing pressure on the Kremlin, Donald Trump is cosying up to Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine. This goes against everything the United States stands for. Congress must act. Every Member of Congress who claims to be outraged by this should join in passing this legislation."
Previously: Twenty-two Democrat and Republican members of the US House of Representatives wrote to Trump demanding the full and immediate implementation of the sanctions against Russia provided for under the Graham Act.
Background:
- In September and October, Trump repeatedly urged Zelenskyy to scale back attacks on Russian oil refineries, linking the strikes to fuel shortages and rising prices in the US.
- On 8 October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that talks would take place in the US involving a Ukrainian delegation. This delegation included Davyd Arakhamiia, leader of the Servant of the People party; Rustem Umierov, Head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service; Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine; and Serhii Kyslytsia, First Deputy Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine.
- Ahead of the meeting, Axios reported, citing US and Ukrainian officials, that US President's Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were planning to present "new ideas and proposals" in Miami to break the diplomatic deadlock.
- On 9 October, Trump said he had had a "highly successful discussion" with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin and reached an agreement on lifting sanctions on Russian diesel fuel.
- US Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick announced that a new bipartisan bill was being prepared to block any purchases of Russian oil. Fitzpatrick's fellow Republican Don Bacon said Trump's decision to purchase Russian diesel fuel looks like weakness.
- On 15 October, the Kremlin announced that Russian diesel fuel had begun reaching global markets following an agreement with Trump.

articles.title: Bulgaria Asks NATO for Aircraft, Air Defenses and Counter-Drone Systems as Black Sea Attacks Intensify

Bulgaria Asks NATO for Aircraft, Air Defenses and Counter-Drone Systems as Black Sea Attacks Intensify
Bulgaria has requested additional aircraft, air defense systems, counter-drone equipment, and air patrols from NATO as attacks on vessels in the Black Sea intensify, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said, according to Novinite on October 16.
Speaking to journalists, Stoyanov warned that the security situation in the Black Sea was deteriorating, with attacks becoming increasingly frequent. He pointed to recent strikes in Romanian territorial waters as evidence of the growing threats facing countries in the region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We have requested aviation, surface-to-air missile systems, counter-drone systems, and air patrols—essentially, the entire spectrum of available assets,” Stoyanov said, adding that the deployment of additional allied resources would also help demonstrate a stronger NATO presence in the region.
However, the minister acknowledged that it remained unclear which capabilities Bulgaria would ultimately receive. He noted that Romania and the Baltic states were facing similar security challenges, while European partners were paying increasing attention to threats in the Black Sea.
“I hope for a swift response and a strengthening of our capabilities,” Stoyanov said.
To improve regional coordination, Bulgaria is also seeking closer cooperation with neighboring NATO members. According to the minister, a meeting involving the defense ministers of Bulgaria, Türkiye, and Romania, alongside the chiefs of defense of all three countries, is expected to take place soon.
The discussions are intended to support the development of a coordinated response to emerging threats and strengthen cooperation among the three Black Sea NATO members.
Despite the requested assistance, Stoyanov cautioned that deploying additional allied forces and equipment would not eliminate all security risks in the region.
“100% security is impossible,” the defense minister said, emphasizing that the objective was to minimize potential threats rather than guarantee complete protection.
Meanwhile, Bulgaria continues to rely on its existing military resources to monitor its maritime territory and respond to potential threats.
According to Stoyanov, the country currently operates two reconnaissance systems dedicated to maritime surveillance, with a third expected to become operational by the end of the year.
The minister said the additional system would introduce technology that had not previously been deployed elsewhere.
The calls for additional security measures follow a series of drone attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, including an incident near Bulgaria’s coast on October 13.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev reported that two commercial vessels had been struck by drones overnight, leaving one ship sunk and forcing the evacuation of the entire crew of another after three drones hit its deck and hull.
One of the vessels was the Chelsea 3, a Ukrainian-owned cargo ship sailing under the Maltese flag, which came under attack approximately 18 nautical miles east of the Bulgarian coastal town of Byala.

articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. As a result of 12 massive Russian strikes this fall, 30 Ukrainian defense industry companies and logistics centers have been hit, thereby significantly reducing Kiev’s ability to produce long-range weapons, including cruise and ballistic missiles, Russian Armed Forces’ General Staff Chief Army General Valery Gerasimov told President Vladimir Putin.

articles.title: UK to Retrofit Donated Weapons for Ukraine With British Sensors, Guidance and EW Systems

UK to Retrofit Donated Weapons for Ukraine With British Sensors, Guidance and EW Systems
Britain plans to retrofit British military technology onto weapons and equipment donated to Ukraine by other countries, while accelerating long-range and air-defense support ahead of winter, UK Defence Journal reported on October 15.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham outlined the plan during talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street. The two also discussed Russia’s continuing attacks on civilians and energy infrastructure following US President Donald Trump’s call for an energy ceasefire, according to the UK government.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to UK Defence Journal, Burnham stated that Britain would continue developing battlefield solutions for Ukraine, including fitting British capabilities onto equipment supplied by other partners.
The approach could involve integrating British sensors, seekers, fuzes, datalinks, or electronic warfare systems with donated hardware. Ukraine has received equipment from more than 50 countries, ranging from Soviet-era systems to modern Western weapons produced to different technical standards.
UK Defence Journal noted that many donated systems lack the communications, guidance, or targeting equipment needed to operate effectively within modern battlefield networks. Retrofitting British components could allow older or incompatible platforms to be integrated more effectively into Ukrainian combat operations.
Burnham and Zelenskyy also discussed accelerating long-range defensive support before winter. Britain intends to continue diplomatic efforts aimed at increasing international supplies of military equipment to Ukraine, the report noted.
The talks also covered a new British package of Lightweight Multirole Missiles designed in part to counter Russia’s growing use of jet-powered drones.
UK Defence Journal highlighted the Geran-3, a jet-powered version of the Iranian-designed Shahed-136 design, as one of the threats driving demand for faster interception systems. The drone’s higher speed reduces the time available to detect and engage it compared with propeller-driven Shaheds.
Lightweight Multirole Missiles are built by Thales in Belfast and can be used against aerial targets including drones. Production is now running at four times its 2022 level, with £100 million ($132.6 million) committed to further expansion, according to the UK Defence Journal.
Britain has already pursued a similar integration model through Stone Cloak, a compact electronic warfare system designed to prevent Russian air defenses from tracking drones. UK Defence Journal reported that the system is produced under a British contract, while its intellectual property has been transferred to Ukraine for domestic mass production.
Britain had already announced a £45 million ($59.7 million) surface-to-air missile package for Ukraine and committed £1.6 billion ($2.12 billion) to deliver more than 5,000 Lightweight Multirole Missiles over four years. Of the new package, £10 million ($13.3 million) is being accelerated to meet Ukraine’s winter air-defense needs.

articles.title: Trump waives ‘bone-crushing’ Russia sanctions
articles.body:
Trump waives ‘bone-crushing’ Russia sanctions
US President Donald Trump has suspended sweeping new sanctions against Russia that he signed into law just a month ago, invoking a national-interest exemption to waive penalties targeting Moscow’s economy and countries purchasing Russian energy.
In an executive order issued on Friday, Trump waived sanctions and tariffs mandated by the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, including proposed 500% tariffs on imports from Russia and 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
“I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States and a report explaining the basis for the certification,” Trump wrote.
China and India, the two largest buyers of Russian crude oil, were expected to be among the countries hardest hit by the legislation.
The bill, championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, has been described by supporters as a “bone-crushing” measure aimed at driving Russian energy exports out of the global market. Hawkish US lawmakers argued that existing restrictions had allowed Moscow to circumvent economic pressure.
Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports earlier this month in an effort to curb rising energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections. The move sparked outrage in Ukraine and among America’s European allies, prompting a bipartisan group of US senators to accuse Trump of betraying Kiev.
According to US media reports, Trump decided to ease sanctions after Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky refused to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities, which Trump blamed for high energy prices.
On Friday, US Representative Gregory Meeks introduced a bill in Congress seeking to block the diesel agreement with Russia. The Democrat accused Trump of “cozying up to [Russian President Vladimir] Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine.”
Trump has defended the agreement as beneficial to American consumers and consistent with his “America First” agenda. In response to the backlash, he attacked Zelensky as “not a good guy for us to deal with” and suggested that Ukraine needed “a new president.”
Russia has maintained that it has adapted to mounting Western economic pressure, while describing the Graham bill as a hostile move that would undermine Trump’s efforts to broker peace between Moscow and Kiev.
“[Russian] diesel has begun reaching global markets, and it will have a certain positive effect on stabilizing oil markets,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Thursday.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s investment envoy and a negotiator on Ukraine, hailed the waiver as “an important and historic moment.” Economic cooperation serves the interests of both countries, “contributes to global economic stability, and lays the foundation for building trust and achieving lasting peace,” he wrote on X.

articles.title: Ukraine in Talks With Trump Envoys Over Energy Truce
articles.body:
Ukrainian officials maintain continuous communication with US President Donald Trump’s special diplomatic envoys to explore mechanisms to halt Russian military aggression, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Saturday, Oct. 17.
Speaking with journalists, Zelensky confirmed that Ukrainian negotiators conducted bilateral discussions with senior White House representatives on Friday, Oct. 16, to coordinate upcoming in-person meetings.

Specifically, National Security and Defense Council Secretary Rustem Umerov held consultations with US special envoy Jared Kushner to establish a timetable and venue for comprehensive negotiations.
“Yesterday our negotiating group was in contact: Umerov spoke with Kushner,” Zelensky said. “They are arranging a meeting, and I am also ready to meet with them.”
Zelensky explained that Kyiv had anticipated convening discussions with American representatives on the sidelines of high-level European summits in Brussels earlier in the week, though that encounter did not materialize. However, the Ukrainian leader affirmed that both teams are working to finalize the format and timing of a bilateral meeting within the coming week.
“We support the possibility of dialogue – anything to stop [Russian President Vladimir] Putin, at least in the format of an energy ceasefire,” Zelensky stated. “It is preferable to end this war completely, but we must start somewhere. At the very least, meetings are necessary, and these meetings are being planned.”
Russia Hits 15 Energy Sites in Massive Strike, Zelensky Says
Diplomatic maneuvering
The diplomatic outreach arrives as Kyiv navigates complex negotiations surrounding prospective truces to shield municipal infrastructure ahead of the winter heating season.
Trump previously declared an immediate “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, asserting that both belligerents had agreed to halt strikes against power grids and petrochemical facilities.
However, implementation mechanisms have remained ambiguous, with Russian forces sustaining long-range missile and drone attacks against Ukrainian electricity generation and transmission infrastructure.
Zelensky has reiterated that Ukraine is prepared to halt asymmetric drone strikes on Russian oil refineries provided Moscow agrees to a reciprocal, verifiable cessation of strikes against Ukrainian municipal energy networks, backed by binding international guarantees.
US envoy contacts
The coordination between Umerov and Kushner follows parallel diplomatic tracks explored by Washington to initiate consultations with the Kremlin.
Earlier in the month, Russian state news agency TASS reported that Kushner alongside fellow US special envoy Steve Witkoff could visit Moscow in mid-to-late October following a telephone discussion between Trump and Putin on Oct. 9.
Following that call, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told Russian state media that Putin rejected resuming formal peace negotiations, asserting that Russian forces hold the operational initiative along the front line and indicating that Moscow intends to continue hostilities until all operational objectives are met.

articles.title: Ukraine could strip critical workers of draft exemptions – PM
articles.body:
Ukraine could strip critical workers of draft exemptions – PM
Ukraine could reduce mobilization exemptions for employees of companies deemed critical to the country, Prime Minister Sergey Koretsky has said, arguing that employers are exploiting the current system.
The country declared mobilization shortly after the escalation of the conflict with Russia in February 2022, barring most military-age men from leaving the country.
However, approximately 1.4 million Ukrainians currently hold employment-based exemptions from military service, according to Economy Minister Aleksandr Kravchenko.
Speaking during a Q&A session in the Ukrainian parliament on Friday, Koretsky said the government is considering stripping critical-sector employers of the right to exempt 100% of their staff. He cited cases in which companies had significantly expanded their workforces, with all employees automatically shielded from conscription.
“Unfortunately, there are many abuses, and additional exemptions continue to be granted every month,” Koretsky said.
“If you have a 100% exemption, it means you can expand your workforce indefinitely and exempt people from mobilization, regardless of whether they actually work as repair technicians, energy workers or in other roles. Unfortunately, this practice has already become widespread,” he added.
Koretsky said some companies had received blanket exemptions despite not meeting the criteria for being classified as critical. As an example, he cited an unnamed contractor for Ukrenergo, the national power grid operator. “When we looked into the details, it turned out that only 20 out of 100 employees were actually working for Ukrenergo. Yet all 100 were exempted,” Koretsky said.
The prime minister called for audits to determine how many employees at a given company perform tasks essential to its operations and the country’s needs. He added that stricter criteria could be applied to businesses as a whole, with only those supporting Ukraine’s defense capabilities and other essential state functions qualifying as critical.
Earlier this week, opposition MP Yaroslav Zhelezhnyak published what he claimed was a draft of the proposed changes, reducing exemption quotas for defense and energy companies from 100% to 85%, and for housing and utility companies from 75% to 60%.
Multiple lawmakers and businesses have warned that such measures would exacerbate existing staffing shortages in critical industries.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian outlet Strana UA reported on Thursday, citing sources, that relations between Koretsky and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky had deteriorated. The outlet claimed that Zelensky could dismiss Koretsky in the spring of 2027 and blame him for government failures during the winter months.
Koretsky, who was appointed prime minister in a government reshuffle in July, has been linked by local media to disgraced businessman and former close Zelensky associate Timur Mindich, who fled to Israel amid an investigation into an alleged $100 million embezzlement scheme involving state nuclear power operator Energoatom.
According to Strana UA, Koretsky has defied Zelensky’s expectations by developing political ambitions, disregarding some of his requests and communicating directly with European partners without Zelensky’s involvement.
Amid mounting battlefield losses and desertions, Ukraine’s conscription drive has been marred by incidents of draft officers forcibly detaining military-age men on the streets, sparking spontaneous protests, clashes and outrage on social media.
While Kiev does not regularly publish figures on its battlefield losses, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk claimed last month that Ukrainian forces had recently been suffering around 27,000 killed and wounded per month. Russia’s Defense Ministry, meanwhile, claimed that Ukrainian casualties reached 500,000 in 2025 alone.

Trump rejects nuclear option against Iran, mentions ‘mother of all bombs’
U.S. President Donald Trump has ruled out using nuclear weapons against Iran, saying the United States can achieve its military objectives without them, while leaving open the possibility of further strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports, citing Anadolu Agency.

articles.title: Iran ships some LPG, jet fuel despite US blockade, data shows
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran ships some LPG, jet fuel despite US blockade, data shows
Iran has managed to export some liquefied petroleum gas and jet fuel since July, despite a US naval blockade, shipping intelligence showed and people involved in security said.
Tehran has in recent weeks been concealing such cargoes among a growing volume of ship-to-ship transfers by other Gulf producers off Oman, news agency Reuters reported- citing four people in maritime security who track Gulf oil movements.
The Iranian exports and methodology are reported for the first time here. While a fraction of its former energy exports, the cargoes are rare evidence of petroleum products getting through a blockade that has halted Iran's crude exports.
Analysis by US advocacy group United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), which monitors Iran-related tanker traffic using ship and satellite tracking, shows at least eight gas tankers carrying Iranian LPG have left the Gulf of Oman since mid-July.
Another tanker carrying Iranian jet fuel reached Myanmar in September, additional satellite imagery and analysis by maritime intelligence group SynMax show.
The US imposed targeted sanctions in 2023 on Myanmar's jet-fuel industry, citing military airstrikes on civilians that the United Nations says have killed thousands of people. Myanmar's military government has repeatedly denied targeting civilians, saying its operations are directed against armed groups.
Six of the eight gas tankers and the jet fuel tanker are under US sanctions for transporting Iranian petroleum and petrochemical products, a Reuters analysis of the vessels and sanctions imposed on ships by the US Treasury showed.
"What we have seen passing is a handful of tankers carrying Iranian LPG, but the overwhelming majority of tankers laden with Iranian products have been redirected by US forces," said Jemima Shelley, senior research analyst with UANI.
Shelley said some Iranian LPG tankers transferred cargoes near the Omani coastal towns of Shinas and Sohar, while others waited in the Gulf of Oman before heading past the US blockade, which US Central Command has said sits across the Gulf of Oman near the Iran-Pakistan border.
The total amount of these LPG cargoes was estimated at 4.1 million barrels, Shelley said.
Shelley said the shipments were driven "more by opportunism" than showing a new trend of Iran trying to export its oil and petrochemicals by using smaller ships.
Most of the cargoes sailed to Malaysia's Eastern Outer Port Limits to conduct further STS transfers for likely destinations in China, Shelley said, based on UANI's analysis.
The Iranian government did not respond to a request for comment. Myanmar's military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment on whether the country had received Iranian jet fuel.
US MILITARY SAYS BLOCKADE 'IRONCLAD'
The US military's Centcom said its naval blockade, which was first imposed on Iran-related oil exports on April 13, is "ironclad". The blockade was lifted in June after the US reached a draft understanding with Iran, but it was reimposed on July 14 following the collapse of the agreement.
Reuters reports, citing a US military official, that the passage of a vessel does not necessarily mean it had evaded the blockade.
Every ship was assessed individually, including through a review of its papers, and some vessels could be allowed through for humanitarian reasons, the official added.
The official said the appearance of a vessel on US sanctions lists is not the only factor to make it subject to the blockade, adding that US forces are also closely monitoring some ships without taking action against them for operational reasons.
Centcom said in an update on October 13 that during the three months of the latest blockade, four commercial vessels had been disabled and 135 ships had been turned around by US forces.
The US military has turned around ships from Asia and also seized some tankers, previous Centcom statements said.
Washington has coupled its blockade with a sanctions campaign aimed at severing Iran's remaining financial links and depriving it of revenue. Last week, it imposed fresh sanctions on 17 vessels involved in transporting Iranian crude, petrochemicals and petroleum products.
A US Treasury spokesperson questioned shipping data suggesting vessels had evaded the blockade, saying ships could spoof their locations or use false identities when loading.
Such data "should be taken with a grain of salt", the spokesperson said.
The Treasury spokesperson said Operation Economic Outcast, together with the blockade, was "suffocating the Iranian regime".
Torbjorn Soltvedt, principal Middle East analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, said although there was no sign of Washington easing its blockade, worsening economic conditions in Iran could push Tehran to take greater risks.
"If Iran can move product tankers through, even in small numbers, jet fuel may be a good option. Iran's aviation industry is under increasing pressure from US sanctions, with a growing number of planes grounded, and a potential surplus of jet fuel at Iranian refineries," Soltvedt added.
Iranian crude exports fell to zero in September, according to Kpler, the first month without a shipment since the analytics firm began tracking the producer in 2013.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the blockade prevented most Chinese purchases of Iranian oil and left Iran unable to deliver crude to customers.

Ukraine’s ADF down four Kalibr missiles, 289 drones in overnight Russian attack

The drones were launched from the directions of Oryol, Bryansk, Kursk and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, as well as temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by Ukrainian aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 8:00 on Saturday, October 17, air defenses had shot down or suppressed 293 targets: four Kalibr cruise missiles; 289 UAVs, including Shahed drones (23 of them jet-powered), S-8000 Banderol drones, Gerbera drones and drones of other types.
Hits were recorded at 22 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at three locations.
The attack is ongoing, with several Russian drones still in Ukrainian airspace.

articles.title: Liberation of DPR, security zone, continuation of massive strikes: Putin’s statements
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. Russia will continue launching strikes against Ukrainian defense enterprises and logistics centers, Russian President Vladimir Putin said while visiting an auxiliary command post of the Joint Force.
He stressed that the establishment of a buffer zone will not be open to discussion with Kiev and thanked Russian troops fighting to liberate Dobropolye and Alexeyevo-Drushkovka in the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR).
TASS has compiled the president’s key statements.
Russia’s objectives
After Ukraine’s incursion into Russia’s Kursk Region, Russian forces were tasked not only with driving the enemy out of Russian territory but also with establishing a security zone, and this task is being successfully implemented: "Our task is to ensure absolute security of Russia’s border territories in the future and we are not going to make this a subject of any potential peace talks with Ukraine."
Commanders of battlegroups must continue "carrying out tasks in strict compliance with the objectives of the special military operation." "Naturally, it is necessary to continue massive and coordinated strikes against enemy defense facilities and logistics centers."
Strikes against the Kiev regime’s facilities have been effective: "I assess the results positively."
"As for the situation on the ground, naturally, one of the key objectives is the liberation of the Donetsk People’s Republic."
Successes
Russian forces are advancing along the entire frontline in the zone of the special military operation, and "the pace of their advance has increased significantly."
Russia’s armed forces continue to carry out the objectives of the special military operation: "As has already been mentioned here, in September alone, more than 1,300 square kilometers of territory in Donbas and Novorossiya was liberated."
"Around 6,500 square kilometers of territory and 310 settlements have been liberated since the beginning of this year."
The liberation of Dobropolye in the DPR is an evident success: "Please convey my words of gratitude to all personnel directly involved in the liberation of Dobropolye. I will say more about this when addressing the commanders of the task forces, but I want to emphasize and point out right here: the capture of Dobropolye is undoubtedly a significant milestone in the liberation of Donbas as a whole and a clear success for the Russian Armed Forces. Congratulations to you all."
"The enemy had turned the city into a fortified stronghold in this area, but the coordinated and highly professional actions of Russian assault units made it possible first to encircle enemy forces in the city and then to take complete control of it."
The liberation of Dobropolye "opens a direct route toward the DPR’s borders."
The liberation of Alexeyevo-Druzhkovka and the start of the assault on Ukrainian fortified areas in Druzhkovka and Kramatorsk in the DPR create conditions for "the swiftest possible completion of the liberation of Donbas from the Kiev regime’s combat units."
"Please convey my most sincere words of gratitude to all the personnel who were directly involved in the liberation of Alexeyevo-Druzhkovka for the courage and resilience they demonstrated during this combat operation."
Russian forces successfully encircled a Ukrainian grouping 2,000 troops in the Kharkov Region: "Entrapping a grouping of about 2,000 troops, in an area of more than 400 square kilometers, 460 square kilometers, is certainly no ordinary feat. Taking into account the subsequent elimination of the enemy in that area, this is indeed a success."
"The offensive in the Zaporozhye Region continues at a high pace, with Battlegroups Dnepr and East’s troops advancing successfully."
"A decisive role [in ensuring rapid progress] undoubtedly belongs to our soldiers and officers, who, while carrying out combat missions, act professionally and demonstrate the finest qualities of the Russian military, such as selfless devotion to the Motherland."
Protection of facilities
Air defense combat crews are operating professionally: "But, of course, there is room for improvement in this regard. We need to enhance the effectiveness of our defense of civilian, first and foremost civilian, and, of course, military facilities."

articles.title: Hypersonic-armed stealth destroyer nears sea trials
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy added $99.1 million to an Ingalls Shipbuilding contract to cover sea trials for USS Lyndon B. Johnson, the last Zumwalt-class destroyer.
- The ship is being fitted in Pascagoula with Conventional Prompt Strike hypersonic missiles, following USS Zumwalt, which finished sea trials in January 2026.
The U.S. Navy is paying Huntington Ingalls Industries another $99.1 million to take USS Lyndon B. Johnson (DDG 1002), the last of its three angular Zumwalt-class stealth destroyers, through sea trials as the ship is fitted to carry hypersonic missiles.
The contract modification, announced by the U.S. Department of War, raises the ceiling on an existing Ingalls Shipbuilding contract to cover the destroyer’s sea trials. About 95% of the work will take place at the company’s shipyard in Pascagoula, Mississippi, with completion scheduled for October 2028, and the U.S. Navy obligated about $59.3 million at signing, split between fiscal 2025 and fiscal 2026 shipbuilding funds.
During sea trials, a new or heavily modified warship leaves the yard to run its propulsion, steering, combat systems and other equipment at sea before the U.S. Navy accepts it. For Lyndon B. Johnson, they will follow years of work in Pascagoula to turn the ship into one of the first U.S. warships able to fire Conventional Prompt Strike, a hypersonic missile designed to reach targets thousands of kilometers away at more than five times the speed of sound.
The Zumwalt class was originally designed around two 155 mm Advanced Gun Systems meant to bombard targets ashore, but the U.S. Navy canceled the guns’ special long-range shells in 2016 after costs soared, leaving the destroyers with guns they could not use, and later decided to remove them and give the three ships a new strike mission with hypersonic missiles.
General Dynamics Bath Iron Works in Maine built Lyndon B. Johnson, which was christened in April 2019 by the late president’s daughters, before moving to Ingalls for combat system activation. In January 2025 the ship entered dry dock in Pascagoula to start installing the large missile tubes for Conventional Prompt Strike, and the U.S. Navy said at the time that it planned to commission the destroyer in 2027.
The lead ship, USS Zumwalt (DDG 1000), went through the same conversion first. Ingalls replaced its forward gun with four large-diameter tubes that each hold three hypersonic missiles, giving the ship 12 in total, and Zumwalt completed builder’s sea trials in January 2026 after nearly three years in the yard, HII said. The second ship, USS Michael Monsoor (DDG 1001), is set to receive the same missile system during a future yard period.
Conventional Prompt Strike shares its hypersonic glide body with the U.S. Army’s Dark Eagle long-range hypersonic weapon, which the U.S. Army fields on truck-mounted launchers. The missile boosts its warhead to high speed and altitude, then releases a glide vehicle that maneuvers toward the target, making it harder for air and missile defenses to intercept. Lockheed Martin, the program’s prime contractor, received a $1.36 billion contract modification earlier this year to support missile and launcher production for the system.
Ingalls is due to finish Lyndon B. Johnson’s sea trials and related work by October 2028, which would make it the second Zumwalt-class destroyer to go to sea with hypersonic missile tubes.

articles.title: Iran manages to ship some gas, jet fuel despite US blockade, sanctions, data shows
articles.body:
Iran has managed to export some liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and jet fuel since July, despite a US naval blockade, shipping intelligence showed and people involved in security said.
Tehran has in recent weeks been concealing such cargoes among a growing volume of ship-to-ship transfers by other Gulf producers off Oman, four people in maritime security who track Gulf oil movements told Reuters.
The Iranian exports and methodology are reported for the first time here. While a fraction of its former energy exports, the cargoes are rare evidence of petroleum products getting through a blockade that has halted Iran's crude exports.
Analysis by US advocacy group United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), which monitors Iran-related tanker traffic using ship and satellite tracking, shows at least eight gas tankers carrying Iranian LPG have left the Gulf of Oman since mid-July.
Another tanker carrying Iranian jet fuel reached Myanmar in September, additional satellite imagery and analysis by maritime intelligence group SynMax show.
The US imposed targeted sanctions in 2023 on Myanmar's jet-fuel industry, citing military airstrikes on civilians that the United Nations says have killed thousands of people. Myanmar's military government has repeatedly denied targeting civilians, saying its operations are directed against armed groups.
Approximately 4.1 million barrels of LPG made it through the blockade
Six of the eight gas tankers and the jet fuel tanker are under US sanctions for transporting Iranian petroleum and petrochemical products, a Reuters analysis of the vessels and sanctions imposed on ships by the US Treasury showed.
"What we have seen passing is a handful of tankers carrying Iranian LPG, but the overwhelming majority of tankers laden with Iranian products have been redirected by US forces," said Jemima Shelley, senior research analyst with UANI.
Shelley said some Iranian LPG tankers transferred cargoes near the Omani coastal towns of Shinas and Sohar, while others waited in the Gulf of Oman before heading past the US blockade, which US Central Command has said sits across the Gulf of Oman near the Iran-Pakistan border.
The total amount of these LPG cargoes was estimated at 4.1 million barrels, Shelley said.
Shelley said the shipments were driven "more by opportunism" than showing a new trend of Iran trying to export its oil and petrochemicals by using smaller ships.
Most of the cargoes sailed to Malaysia's Eastern Outer Port Limits to conduct further STS transfers for likely destinations in China, Shelley said, based on UANI's analysis.
The Iranian government did not respond to a request for comment. Myanmar's military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment on whether the country had received Iranian jet fuel.
US Military describes blockade as 'ironclad'
The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) said its naval blockade, which was first imposed on Iran-related oil exports on April 13, is "ironclad." The blockade was lifted in June after the US reached a draft understanding with Iran, but it was reimposed on July 14 following the collapse of the agreement.
A US military official told Reuters that the passage of a vessel does not necessarily mean it had evaded the blockade. Every ship was assessed individually, including through a review of its papers, and some vessels could be allowed through for humanitarian reasons, the official added.
The official said the appearance of a vessel on US sanctions lists is not the only factor to make it subject to the blockade, adding that US forces are also closely monitoring some ships without taking action against them for operational reasons.
Centcom said in an update on October 13 that during the three months of the latest blockade, four commercial vessels had been disabled and 135 ships had been turned around by US forces.
The US military has turned around ships from Asia and also seized some tankers, previous Centcom statements said.
Washington has coupled its blockade with a sanctions campaign aimed at severing Iran's remaining financial links and depriving it of revenue. Last week, it imposed fresh sanctions on 17 vessels involved in transporting Iranian crude, petrochemicals and petroleum products.
US Treasury questioned shipping data
A US Treasury spokesperson questioned shipping data suggesting vessels had evaded the blockade, saying ships could spoof their locations or use false identities when loading.
Such data "should be taken with a grain of salt," the spokesperson said.
The Treasury spokesperson said Operation Economic Outcast, together with the blockade, was "suffocating the Iranian regime."
Torbjorn Soltvedt, principal Middle East analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, said although there was no sign of Washington easing its blockade, worsening economic conditions in Iran could push Tehran to take greater risks.
"If Iran can move product tankers through, even in small numbers, jet fuel may be a good option. Iran's aviation industry is under increasing pressure from US sanctions, with a growing number of planes grounded, and a potential surplus of jet fuel at Iranian refineries," Soltvedt added.
Iranian crude exports fell to zero in September, according to Kpler, the first month without a shipment since the analytics firm began tracking the producer in 2013.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the blockade prevented most Chinese purchases of Iranian oil and left Iran unable to deliver crude to customers.

articles.title: Russian night attacks on Ukrainian regions: one person killed in Kherson, dozens injured, and infrastructure damaged
articles.body:
Russian night attacks on Ukrainian regions: one person killed in Kherson, dozens injured, and infrastructure damaged
Kyiv • UNN
Russia attacked a number of regions in Ukraine with missiles, aircraft, and drones. An ambulance driver was killed, and dozens of people, including children, were injured.
During the night of October 17 and in the morning, Russian forces carried out a series of missile, air, and drone attacks on Ukrainian regions. Kharkiv, Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih, Sumy region, and other regions came under attack. One person was reported killed, dozens injured, including children, and residential buildings and industrial facilities were damaged. This was reported by local military administrations, police, and rescuers, UNN writes.
Details
In Kherson, Russian aircraft attacked the Korabelnyi district on the morning of October 17. According to Yarоslav Shanko, head of the city military administration, a 64-year-old ambulance driver was killed. Among those injured were an 11-year-old girl and a family with a one-month-old infant. A paramedic was also injured during a repeated strike.
In Zaporizhzhia, the Russians struck a residential area. According to the regional military administration, five people, including a child, were injured. Apartment buildings were damaged, and cars caught fire as a result of the attack.
Mass strikes on Kharkiv, Sumy region, and the central regions
In Kharkiv, 15 people, including three children, were injured as a result of a missile attack on the evening of October 16. One of the strikes hit a warehouse building in the Nemyshlianskyi district, where a fire covering an area of 100 square meters broke out. Nearby high-rise buildings were damaged, and rescuers extinguished four fires.
In the Sumy region, 25 Russian shelling attacks were recorded over the course of the day, with 19 settlements coming under fire. According to the police, eight people were injured. In the Sumy community, six residents sustained injuries and trauma, while another woman suffered an acute stress reaction. In the Znob-Novhorodske community, a 52-year-old woman was injured as a result of a drone strike.
In Kryvyi Rih, Russian forces attacked an industrial enterprise. In Dnipro, according to local authorities, a combined attack involving ballistic and cruise missiles was recorded. Explosions were also reported in Zhytomyr and the Chernivtsi region.
Explosions were also heard in the Khmelnytskyi region, where widespread power outages were reported in the northern part of the region. Meanwhile, in the Cherkasy region, air defense forces neutralized six Russian drones during October 16–17. Information about the consequences of the attacks in certain regions is still being clarified.

articles.title: Trump backs Israel unity plan keeping Netanyahu PM for two years
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump backs Israel unity plan keeping Netanyahu PM for two years after election: Report
The Trump administration is backing efforts to form a broad Israeli unity government after this month's election that could keep Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister for up to two years before handing power to opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, according to an Israeli media report.
The proposal would exclude far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and bring together Netanyahu's Likud party with Eisenkot's Yashar party, Israel Hayom reported on Friday.
The newspaper cited unnamed US and foreign political officials familiar with the discussions. Neither Washington nor the Israeli parties involved have publicly confirmed an agreed plan.
Israel is due to hold a Knesset election on 27 October.
Polls have suggested neither Netanyahu's right-wing bloc nor the fragmented opposition is guaranteed a stable governing majority, raising the possibility of prolonged coalition negotiations.
According to Israel Hayom, the US and regional governments believe a broad coalition would be better placed to make major decisions on ending regional conflicts and advancing President Donald Trump's wider Middle East agenda.
One unnamed foreign official quoted in the report said a fragile minority government would be unable to make the "major and decisive political decisions" the region required.
The proposed arrangement would allow Netanyahu to remain prime minister for up to two years before Eisenkot succeeded him, according to the report.
During that period, the government would be expected to work towards ending wars on multiple fronts and reaching political agreements with regional states, particularly Saudi Arabia.
The Trump administration has been pushing Riyadh to join the Abraham Accords and normalise relations with Israel.
Washington has linked that effort to other parts of the US-Saudi relationship, including F-35 fighter jets and a civilian nuclear programme.
Saudi officials have repeatedly said, however, that normalisation with Israel would require meaningful progress towards Palestinian statehood.
The issue has also become entangled with Washington's proposed nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia, which Trump has said would depend on Riyadh joining the Abraham Accords.
According to Israel Hayom, Saudi Arabia is also seeking a different political configuration in Israel before moving forward.
US Ambassador Mike Huckabee has recently met several senior Israeli politicians, including Eisenkot, the report said.
The contacts were said to have been handled carefully because of concerns over perceptions of US interference in the election.
But Israeli politicians were reportedly told that Washington and other governments would welcome a broad and stable coalition without far-right parties.
Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, has emerged as one of Netanyahu's principal challengers in the election and leads the centrist Yashar party.
The proposed government would also seek to address domestic issues that have deeply divided Israeli politics.
These include demands for an official inquiry into the failures surrounding the 7 October 2023 attacks, disputes over the judiciary and the continuing row over exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog has denied reports that he is directly involved in efforts to engineer a unity government.
He has nevertheless said he wants to avoid repeated elections and see a stable government formed after the vote.
The reported US effort comes as Israel's election remains highly fragmented, with Palestinian parties potentially playing a decisive role if neither major bloc secures a governing majority.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits Russian Rail Bridge, Ammunition Warehouses
articles.body:
Ukrainian Defense Forces have struck a strategic railway bridge inside Russia’s Bryansk region, alongside multiple military logistics depots and a drone command post across occupied Donetsk region.
According to an official dispatch released by the General Staff, precision strikes were conducted throughout Friday, Oct. 16, and overnight into Saturday morning, targeting logistical nodes that sustain Russian military formations.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Inside Russia, Ukrainian fire engaged a railway bridge spanning the Unecha River near the settlement of Sloboda-Seletska in the Bryansk region.
Ukrainian defense planners noted that severing or degrading the crossing is engineered to disrupt Russian military rail transport, specifically interdicting shipments of ammunition, petroleum products, and heavy combat vehicles toward frontline formations.
“Damage was recorded to a railway bridge across the Unecha River in the area of Sloboda-Seletska, Bryansk region of the Russian Federation,” the General Staff announced.
“This will complicate rail logistics for Russian forces, in particular the supply of ammunition, fuel, and military equipment.”
Depots and drone control posts hit in occupied Donetsk region
Simultaneously, Ukrainian precision units targeted rear logistics hubs and unmanned aviation command installations across Russian-occupied sectors of the Donetsk region.
Military authorities confirmed direct impacts on Russian material and technical supply warehouses in the areas of Novoandriivka, Mykilske, and the port city of Mariupol.
Zelensky: ‘Putin’s Real Enemy Is the Rules-Based Order’ – Key Takeaways From Brussels
The destruction of concentrated storage depots restricts frontline Russian tactical groups from rapidly replenishing ammunition, vehicular parts, and fuel reserves along contested southern and eastern sectors.
In the vicinity of Malynivka in the Donetsk region, Ukrainian fire struck an active Russian unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) command and control post, suppressing enemy drone reconnaissance and strike coordination.
The General Staff emphasized that systematic interdiction of transport arteries, supply bases, and drone command centers forms part of a sustained campaign to degrade the combat potential and logistical stamina of Russian forces.
Asymmetric interdiction of supply corridors
The strikes across the Bryansk and Donetsk regions follow an expanding Ukrainian operational effort to dismantle critical transport bridges and chokepoints linking Russian staging bases with occupied Ukrainian territory.
In late September, Ukrainian strikes damaged the Chonhar road bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russian-held sectors of the Kherson region. Independent open-source satellite intelligence published by Dnipro OSINT showed that consecutive precision strikes blasted large craters into the roadway before causing a full bridge span to collapse by Sept. 30.
The collapse of the Chonhar span severely constrained Russian vehicular transport between the Crimean peninsula and occupied southern Ukraine, forcing Russian military logistics units onto longer, more vulnerable detours along the Sea of Azov coastal corridor.

articles.title: Drone Attack Paralyzes Moscow Airports Again
articles.body:
A major wave of Ukrainian strike drones targeted the Moscow region and multiple regions early Saturday morning, Oct. 17, forcing civil aviation authorities to shut down airspace across the Russian capital and divert international flights to alternative hubs.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin reported that Russian air defense units intercepted 75 unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) heading toward the metropolitan capital. Sobyanin stated that municipal emergency services and defense specialists deployed to the sites of falling debris, without specifying the intended targets of the drone strikes.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The aerial incursions prompted Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency, Rosaviatsiya, to enact emergency ground stops and flight restrictions across Moscow’s primary airport cluster shortly before midnight.
Among the disrupted commercial flights was a Pegasus Airlines flight transiting from Antalya, Turkey, to Moscow. Passengers reported departing Turkey at 7:35 p.m., only to be informed prior to descent that the airspace above Moscow had been sealed.
The airliner diverted to Pulkovo Airport in St. Petersburg, landing at approximately 1:00 a.m. local time, where passengers were instructed to remain on board until Moscow airspace reopened.
Similar flight restrictions and ground delays were instituted across regional air hubs in western Russia as air raid warnings sounded.
Ministry claims 610 drones intercepted across 15 regions
According to an operational bulletin issued by the Russian Ministry of Defense, Russian air defenses intercepted and destroyed 610 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones across the country between Friday evening and Saturday morning.
Meeks Introduces Bill to Block Trump-Putin Diesel Deal
The ministry claimed the overnight wave engaged targets across a broad geographical footprint spanning 15 administrative regions alongside occupied territories.
Regions targeted included the Moscow region, Leningrad, Novgorod, Tver, Bryansk, Belgorod, Kursk, Oryol, Kaluga, Voronezh, Rostov, Smolensk, and Tula regions, as well as the Krasnodar region, the Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug in western Siberia, and occupied Crimea.
Compounding disruptions to Russian civil aviation
The Saturday morning aviation shutdown marks the third time in ten days that drone alerts paralyzed Moscow’s airspace.
Overnight into Friday, Oct. 16, Moscow’s four primary airports – Vnukovo, Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovsky – suspended all inbound and outbound flights, forcing more than 20 commercial airliners to divert to alternate airports and causing over 200 flight cancellations before restrictions were lifted around 5:45 a.m. local time.
That disruption followed an earlier overnight shutdown on Oct. 13–14, during which more than 500 flights were delayed or canceled across the capital’s hubs.
Civil aviation data released by Rosaviatsiya head Dmitry Yadrov indicates that recurring airspace closures and drone threats have contracted commercial passenger traffic, with Russian carriers transporting 39.5 million passengers between May and August – a 7 percent decline compared to 42.6 million passengers carried during the corresponding period in 2025.
Ukrainian officials have stated that interdiction operations do not target civilian aircraft, but aim to constrain military transport and highlight the risks of utilizing Russian sovereign airspace during wartime.
In September, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned international air carriers and insurers of escalating hazards across Russian skies, stating that active airfields and logistics nodes supporting Moscow’s war effort remain valid operational targets.

Russia could be preparing to escalate its hybrid attacks against Poland “before Christmas Eve,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned.

The Polish prime minister made the remarks during a press briefing after a European Council summit in Brussels.
Large-scale provocations
Tusk said the risks would be particularly acute around borders and railway lines used to transport essential supplies to Ukraine, including gas, oil and food.
He also warned that Poland could face more sabotage attempts and provocations.
“We should expect, as we have so far, but on a larger scale, attempts at sabotage or provocations in Poland,” he said, adding that the threat also extended to the three Baltic states.
“One message is clear: Russia will intensify this escalation and test our response. That is the problem,” he added.
Europe has been on heightened alert in recent months following intelligence assessments warning that Russia could test NATO through sabotage, cyberattacks, drone activity or even a limited military operation.

articles.title: Polish military to practise deploying forces in Ukraine in event of ceasefire with Russia – media

Polish military to practise deploying forces in Ukraine in event of ceasefire with Russia – media
According to The Times, 1,500 European troops will practise deploying forces to Ukraine in Poland in November in preparation for a possible ceasefire with Russia.
Source: European Pravda, citing The Times
Details: The exercises are said to be the first of their kind. They will focus on preparing for the post-war situation, in which the presence of European troops on Ukrainian territory would serve as a deterrent.
Soldiers from several countries, including France and Germany, will practise troop movements and logistical support as part of a multinational peacekeeping operation.
The publication learned that at least 1,500 British, French and German troops, along with the Polish Armed Forces, will take part in the exercises.
A source in the UK Ministry of Defence said that troops would rehearse a scenario in which "multinational forces are together in a particular area", but declined to provide further details.
A senior Polish official said the exercises would underscore the unity of Europe's major military powers in the face of the Russian threat and the need to continue supporting Ukraine.
UK Defence Secretary John Healey said in Washington that next month, "thousands of troops will take part in major exercises in Poland to ensure we are ready to support the military training and post-war reconstruction that Ukraine will need".
He made the remarks following his first in-person meeting with his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon.
Background:
- The exercises were agreed upon at a summit in Paris in July and announced by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
- The Coalition of the Willing, led by France and the UK, is working on a plan to deploy a mission to Ukraine to guarantee a future ceasefire.

articles.title: IRGC say tanker exploded after hitting mine in Hormuz strait
articles.body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards on Saturday said an oil tanker was on fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine in the waterway at the heart of the Middle East war.
Tehran seized control over Hormuz after the start of the war in late February, choking off the strait that normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption.
