articles.title: EU vows satellite support for Ukraine but cannot yet replace Starlink
articles.body:
The European Union has pledged to help Ukraine reduce its dependence on US-owned satellite communications, while acknowledging that it cannot replace Starlink in the short term.
Speaking at an EU summit in Brussels on Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said services were still being restored after disruptions he described as “a very unpleasant and dangerous surprise”.
Ukraine reported restrictions this week on some Starlink internet terminals, saying they had hampered its ability to defend against Russian forces.
The disruption came amid renewed tensions between Kiev and Washington even as US President Donald Trump denied ordering temporary disruption of Starlink service for Ukraine’s military.
EU leaders rallied around Zelenskyy but acknowledged limits to the support Europe could immediately provide.
“We are working hard to help Ukraine strengthen its ability to defend itself through satellite imagery and early-warning systems, which are much needed,” French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters after the talks.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that Europe had no readily available replacement.
“Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine, and unfortunately in the short term Europe can’t replace this capability,” she said.
Europe’s satellite plans
EU countries currently pool and share satellite communications capacity through GOVSATCOM, a programme in which the bloc wants to fully include Ukraine, EU spokesperson Thomas Regnier said.
The EU also plans to incorporate commercial services into GOVSATCOM early next year to help meet military needs while it develops its own satellite network.
That network, known as IRIS², is intended to rival Starlink. Launches are planned for 2029, with full operations targeted for 2030.
Ukraine uses SpaceX’s military satellite service, Starshield, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-controlled territory and interceptor drones.
It also uses the company’s civilian Starlink system, though not for offensive operations.
SpaceX owner Elon Musk, whose stance on Ukraine has shifted repeatedly since 2022, said this week that any disruption was the responsibility of the US government, not his company.
Limited alternatives
European support extends beyond EU programmes. France’s Eutelsat already provides satellite communications services to Ukraine through its OneWeb network, although it has disclosed little about government and military uses.
Its constellation of 648 satellites, however, is far smaller than Starlink’s network of more than 10,000.
According to specialist publication Via Satellite, OneWeb cannot support drone and ground robot operations because of limited capacity and a lack of compact satellite terminals.
Kallas said the European Defence Agency had identified critical capabilities that Europe lacked, stressing that those gaps needed to be filled “as soon as possible”.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs also underscored Ukraine’s dependence on the service.
“Starlink is the key for Ukraine, actually, to fight or fight back,” he told reporters. “It takes time for us to have the same capabilities. We do have it, but not enough.”
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said he had discussed Starlink with Macron on Thursday, including how European countries could provide more such services in the near future.

articles.title: Trump-Putin diesel deal fractures West on Russia – ex-Austrian FM
articles.body:
Trump-Putin diesel deal fractures West on Russia – ex-Austrian FM
Washington’s diesel deal with Moscow has exposed divisions within the West over its anti-Russian stance, as the US shifts toward a more pragmatic approach, former Austrian Foreign Minister Karin Kneissl has said.
US President Donald Trump announced the agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week, easing sanctions on Russian diesel imports until April 2027 in an effort to bring down soaring fuel prices. The move marks a departure from the Western sanctions policy imposed on Moscow since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022.
Speaking to TASS on Friday, Kneissl described the agreement as more than a “symbolic breakthrough,” pointing to the 300,000 tons of Russian diesel expected to reach the US and global markets by November.
“The EU says that this undermines the West’s united position. However, one could also say that this marks a shift by the US toward a more pragmatic approach, while the EU continues to pursue a purely ideological line,” she stated.
The agreement has drawn criticism from European leaders attending a two-day EU summit in Brussels this week. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis accused Trump of sidelining the bloc, telling reporters that “Trump, by doing that business with Putin, stabbed us in the back. We have to do something.”
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, however, welcomed the agreement, arguing that lower fuel prices were essential to Europe’s economic competitiveness. “Any step in reducing fuel prices and to guarantee our competitiveness, we appreciate,” he said.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas described the agreement as a “gift to Putin,” while defending Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reaffirmed on Friday that the bloc would maintain its sanctions against Moscow despite Washington’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel.
Brussels’ hardline stance contrasts with that of EU member Slovakia, which remains heavily dependent on Russian energy and has sought to maintain economic ties with Moscow. Prime Minister Robert Fico has repeatedly called for diplomacy rather than continued military support for Kiev.
The dispute has also strained relations between Washington and Kiev. Trump has repeatedly urged Vladimir Zelensky to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, blaming the attacks for pushing up global fuel prices.
Zelensky criticized the diesel agreement as a “weak decision” and accused Trump of “betrayal.” Ukraine continued targeting Russian energy facilities, including a refinery in Ryazan Region on Thursday, prompting Trump to condemn the attacks as a “disgrace.” At Friday’s summit, Zelensky sought additional financial and military assistance from European leaders but left empty-handed, with only renewed promises of support.
The confrontation comes as global diesel supplies remain under pressure from the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The International Energy Agency agreed on Thursday to accelerate the release of emergency oil reserves, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel, in an effort to ease shortages and bring down prices.

articles.title: How Iran messaging highlights cost of war ahead of US midterm elections
articles.body:
How Iran messaging highlights cost of war ahead of US midterm elections
Through statements in English, Iranian officials are emphasising gas prices and issues with the US economy.
In messages that appear to be directed at the American public, Iran has been highlighting the cost of the war that the United States and Israel launched against the country ahead of the United States midterm elections.
Iranian officials have published articles in state-affiliated outlets stressing the disastrous impact of the war on oil prices and the US economy, while Iran’s chief negotiator and Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has actively targeted US officials about rising costs and military spending.
Sina Toossi, a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, said Tehran is looking to increase the political cost of the war for Trump by trying to talk directly to the American public.
“It’s not necessarily that they’re trying to get Democrats in power or manipulate US politics in a certain direction, other than just overall increasing the costs on this issue of the Iran war, and just playing that game of information warfare and getting out their own narrative and propaganda as well,” Toossi told Al Jazeera.
Trump’s Republican Party is looking to retain control of the Senate and House of Representatives in next month’s midterm vote. But the Democratic Party, which largely opposes the war with Iran, is mounting a strong challenge across the congressional electoral map, including in areas that have been conservative strongholds for decades, such as Texas.
On Wednesday, Ghalibaf shared a news story on inflation rising to 3.7 percent last month along with a collage of negative headlines on the US economy.
The social media post also featured a comic strip from the Road Runner cartoon showing Wile E Coyote building a catapult that misfires and launches a boulder at him.
“Let’s ‘play the percentages’. Not in odds, but in the % increases,” Ghalibaf wrote in a message to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has been leading the sanctions campaign against Iran.
Bessent said last month that he represents “the house”, likening the economy to a casino while addressing the national debt and bond market.
Ghalibaf’s remark referred to the increase in inflation, underscoring that the cost of living keeps rising due to the war despite Bessent’s assertions.
Days earlier, he shared an image of a ghost shaped like a bell curve, with diesel prices rising and housing affordability and consumer confidence falling.
Since the start of the war on February 28, Iran has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, sending energy prices soaring. In the US, the price of diesel is at an all-time record of $6.33 per gallon (3.8 litres), according to the American Automobile Association, and gas is $4.33, up from less than $3 before the war.
Iran has intensified its attacks on vessels around the strait in recent days after Trump and his aides repeatedly stressed that the waterway is under US control.
The uptick in energy prices has fuelled overall inflation in the economy, leading the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates last month at a time when Trump has been calling for them to be cut to stimulate economic activity.
In a letter to the American public on September 29, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) accused Trump of lying about the cost of the war and the state of the US economy, dismissing the president’s claims that oil prices would soon nosedive.
“Countries around the world have lost their faith in the US economy. Demand for American bonds has plummeted. In fact, countries are starting to offload their US bonds. Soon, the dam will break, and the economy will implode, causing, unfortunately, great pain for Americans for many many years,” the IRGC said.
“Americans need to wake up. They need to wrest control back from corrupt politicians. Now is the time, as the American political system is at its weakest.”
The US midterm elections are seen as a turning point in the conflict – not because of their potential outcome, but because of what Trump might do after the vote.
Trump has suggested that he would either strike a deal with Iran or return to a full-scale war after the November 3 legislative elections. He has also dismissed the idea that the vote will have any impact on his Iran policy.
“They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don’t realise is that I’m not running,” Trump said at the United Nations General Assembly last month.
“I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election. When it comes to Iran, it doesn’t even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”
If the Democrats gain control of Congress, they can push for measures to curb Trump’s ability to continue the war, including through withholding funding for the military campaign.
But Toossi said there is a debate within Iran on the potential impact of a Democratic victory in November.
While some point to foreign policy hawks among the Democrats to argue that little would change, others say a midterm defeat would make him politically vulnerable and likely constrain his war powers.
“I don’t think they’re hedging their bets either way, and I don’t think it necessarily affects their overall strategy of increasing the costs [of war] regardless of whatever happens in November,” Toossi told Al Jazeera.

Zelensky explains how Ukraine uses Starlink to intercept Shahed drones
According to him, after Starlink’s performance was reduced, the Ukrainian military lost the ability to intercept some of these targets.
He made this announcement during a press conference in Brussels, according to Ukrinform.
“We sometimes imagine that Starlink is used by the Armed Forces of Ukraine to carry out precision strikes. No. We do not use Starlink to attack or respond within the territory of the Russian Federation. That is precisely why we appealed to SpaceX and the White House to grant us this capability. If we had it, we wouldn’t have had to ask,” Zelensky said.
He explained that Ukraine uses Starlink to operate interceptor drones that destroy “Shahed” rockets attacking the civilian population, and called the speed restrictions on the system an unpleasant and dangerous surprise.
“That’s why they didn’t shut down Starlink, but reduced its speed, and when they reduced the speed, we were unable to shoot down a certain number of ‘Jet-Shaheds.’ This is very unpleasant. We were unable to use it [the tool] to protect the population. This is very painful and unpleasant. The ‘Jet Shahids’ were traveling at speeds of over 400 km, but they reduced our speed to 70…,” the President said.
As reported by Ukrinform, Serhiy “Flash” Beskrestnov, a special advisor to the President on technological issues, stated that SpaceX imposed speed limits on Starlink terminals while in motion overnight, and the Ukrainian Defense Forces did not receive any warning.
A source in the Ministry of Defense also reported that the Starlink operational restrictions detected overnight complicated the work of unmanned systems, logistics, and the Defense Forces’ “middle strike” operations.
In addition, the President’s special advisor on technology, Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, emphasized that by limiting the operating speed of Starlink terminals, SpaceX is effectively depriving Ukraine of the ability to defend itself against “Shahed” drones.

articles.title: US move to restart direct flights with Lebanon hits roadblock
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump move to restart direct US flights with Lebanon hits roadblock
The United Nations aviation agency has found Lebanon's main airport lacks valid certification, according to a report summary, in a setback to US President Donald Trump's move to revive direct US-Beirut flights.
Trump made the announcement in July and signed an order last month for the US government to allow direct flights from the US to Lebanon, reversing a four-decade-long suspension after TWA Flight 847 was hijacked and forced to land in Beirut in 1985.
While the US Federal Aviation Administration and the Transportation Security Administration would still need to conduct safety reviews before flights could resume, the Lebanese embassy in Washington called Trump's order "a significant first step toward restoring direct air service between Lebanon and the United States."
However, the UN's International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) technical assistance mission to Lebanon in July identified shortcomings at Beirut-Rafic Hariri International Airport and in the aviation system.
The findings, which two senior industry officials familiar with the matter expect to delay the resumption of service, complicate efforts to follow up on an order Trump signed after meeting Lebanese President Joseph Aoun. Washington has backed Aoun as it pushes for Iran-backed Hezbollah to be disarmed.
The agency sent its internal report, made at the request of the Lebanese Civil Aviation Authority (LCAA), to Lebanon in September.
AIRPORT LACKS EMERGENCY PLAN: ICAO
Beirut airport's firefighting resources are equipped for single-aisle planes, but not twin-aisle jetliners used for long-haul flights, according to a summary of ICAO's report. The airport also lacks an emergency plan, and its conditional certification has expired, the report said.
"This is a serious and time-critical matter that must be addressed immediately to preserve the airport's operational status," the summary said.
The report also found the Lebanese regulator LCAA lacks qualified inspectors to oversee air traffic control licensing, and has no fully established, operational and independent aircraft accident investigation authority with clearly defined roles.
Such concerns were flagged during a two-day workshop last month where officials from ICAO, Lebanon's government, the FAA and others discussed efforts to revive direct air service, according to the industry officials and an agenda of the meeting seen by Reuters.
Lebanon's Minister of Public Works and Transport Fayez Rasamny said Lebanon was taking steps to address the concerns, with efforts to certify the airport starting on Saturday. The LCAA expects to issue conditional certification in the coming days.
"Most of the issues highlighted in the report had already been identified by the LCAA, and corrective action had already been initiated," Rasamny said in a statement, adding that progress had been delayed by war.
Israeli forces remain in southern Lebanon and have continued strikes despite a US-brokered framework agreement signed in June between Israel and Lebanon.
Hezbollah, which was not party to the deal, has rejected it.
The FAA declined to comment. ICAO said it cannot comment on matters concerning specific countries, but said it conducts targeted analyses for member states.
The US State Department advises Americans not to travel to Lebanon given safety concerns. It said the FAA advises caution for flights operating in Lebanese airspace due to heightened military activity in or around Syria, including the risks of errant long-range surface-to-air missiles originating from Syrian territory.
MIDDLE EAST UNREST DISRUPTS AIR TRAVEL
Foreign airlines have avoided large swathes of Middle East airspace because of missile and drone threats since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February triggered regional hostilities, with an airport in Saudi Arabia the latest site to come under attack.
Lebanon and its national carrier have been praised domestically for maintaining air navigation services and flights, helping to prop up an economy that depends on tourism and remittances.
Reuters reported, citing three US airline officials on the condition of anonymity, they do not think any American carriers would resume flights to Lebanon in the near term due to security concerns.
While there are no direct flights between Beirut and the United States, such service exists between Lebanon and some large European cities.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency said it was aware of the ICAO report and added that EU airlines must conduct their own assessment of an airport's safety and operational readiness before launching services.

articles.title: Russia, US eye new joint projects as diesel deal faces sanctions hurdles
articles.body:
Russia and the United States are preparing to unveil new economic initiatives, including potential nuclear-powered data centers, as Washington seeks to overcome sanctions-related obstacles to a recently announced Russian diesel deal, a senior Kremlin envoy said Friday.
Kirill Dmitriev, President Vladimir Putin's special envoy for investment and economic cooperation, said Moscow and Washington were exploring several areas of collaboration that could move forward even before the war in Ukraine ends.
Speaking at the Russian Energy Week conference in Moscow, Dmitriev said discussions included joint data center projects that could use electricity generated by Russian nuclear power plants.
He said additional initiatives would be announced soon, describing the diesel agreement reached between U.S. President Donald Trump and Putin as a potential model for broader economic cooperation.
The developments come as the two countries navigate a complex sanctions landscape that threatens to complicate efforts to expand commercial ties.
Dmitriev said the U.S. Treasury Department had approached the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), which he heads, for assistance in resolving payment difficulties linked to the diesel agreement.
According to Dmitriev, Washington asked the fund to facilitate transactions and address technical obstacles that could hinder implementation.
The RDIF would work to ensure payments were processed efficiently and reached their intended recipients, he said.
The agreement, announced by Trump last week, would allow Russian diesel to reach U.S. and international markets in an effort to lower fuel prices ahead of November's U.S. midterm elections.
Lower energy costs have become a key political priority for Trump, but the arrangement has drawn sharp criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and raised questions about the future of U.S. sanctions targeting Russian oil.
Implementing the deal would require Washington to ease certain restrictions, including measures imposed by the Trump administration itself.
Dmitriev acknowledged that overlapping sanctions had created considerable uncertainty over how the agreement could proceed.
"There are so many layers of sanctions piled on top of one another that everyone has become confused," he said, adding that U.S. officials were examining ways to remove the relevant restrictions.
He said discussions were already underway on possible sanctions relief, suggesting that Washington was actively seeking a workable solution.
However, Dmitriev warned that a separate U.S. sanctions and tariff measure, known as the Graham Act, could effectively shut down broader investment cooperation between the two countries.
The legislation, introduced by the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham, is intended to intensify economic pressure on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
Dmitriev argued that the measure would undermine potential Russian-American business ventures and limit both countries' ability to cooperate in stabilizing global energy markets.
He maintained that economic engagement could proceed alongside diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, with the diesel agreement potentially opening the door to additional projects.
The discussions underscore Moscow's push to revive commercial ties with Washington despite continuing tensions over Ukraine and extensive sanctions imposed on Russia.
While Dmitriev expressed optimism about further agreements, the proposed initiatives remain subject to significant legal and political hurdles as Washington weighs economic cooperation against its existing sanctions framework.

articles.title: Belgium to deliver 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by end of year — PM
articles.body:
BRUSSELS, October 16. /TASS/. Belgium intends to transfer ten F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of this year, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever said following a meeting with Vladimir Zelensky on the sidelines of the EU summit in Brussels.
"Ukraine urgently needs operational jets (…), and we can help with that. <...> We will supply ten [aircraft] this year," the Belga news agency quoted De Wever as saying.
The Belgian prime minister noted that the schedule for the transfer of military equipment had been pushed back due to delays in the delivery of American F-35 fighters to Belgium, which are intended to replace the F-16s currently in service with the country’s air force.
Belgium has promised to deliver its first two F-16s to Ukraine in 2024, and then to transfer all remaining operational aircraft in phases. In June 2026, Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken announced plans to transfer seven F-16 fighter jets by the end of this year. To date, deliveries have not begun due to delays in receiving the F-35s.
The Belgian F-16s are, on average, about 40 years old. The Belgian Air Force has about 200 aircraft on its roster, however, according to local media estimates, no more than 40 remain operational.

articles.title: Trump Says He Would Like to See Putin at G20 Summit
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump said he is uncertain whether Russian President Vladimir Putin will attend the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami this December, but stated that he “would love to have him” at the gathering.
Responding to questions from journalists regarding Putin’s prospective participation, Trump confirmed that the Russian leader’s attendance remains unconfirmed, Forbes TV News reported on Saturday, Oct. 17.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I don’t know if he’s coming. I would love to have him, certainly,” Trump told reporters.
The remarks follow earlier statements from the White House indicating an openness to hosting the Russian leader at the multilateral summit, which is scheduled to convene in Florida in December.
The prospective invitation has emerged as a point of contention among Western allies and European institutions, who have maintained an international diplomatic boycott of the Russian head of state since the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
President Trump:
"I don't know" if Putin will be attending G-20 Summit in Miami pic.twitter.com/aT4FTQ8dVZ
— Forbes Breaking News (@ForbesTVNews) October 16, 2026
European pushback
Trump’s openness to hosting Putin in Miami has drawn sharp criticism from European officials.
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas previously condemned the diplomatic invitation, pointing to state-sponsored security threats and criminal indictments unsealed in the US involving Russian intelligence operations.
Kallas highlighted a September indictment by the US Department of Justice charging individuals linked to Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) with plotting the contract assassination of a prominent Russian dissident on American soil.
Trump Denies Role in Slowing Ukraine’s Military Starlink
“Trump’s inviting Putin to the G20 was very hard to hear,” Kallas stated, arguing that hostile intelligence activities operate under direct instructions from the Kremlin.
The European Commission confirmed that the EU will use the Miami summit to condemn Russia’s military aggression against Ukraine, regardless of whether Putin travels to the event.
Commission deputy chief spokesperson Olof Gill emphasized that the 27-nation bloc has utilized every G20 platform since 2022 to demand the cessation of hostilities, reiterating that the stance will continue “irrespective of the participants at any G20 meeting.”
Any potential international travel by Putin also intersects with legal obligations surrounding the International Criminal Court (ICC), which issued an arrest warrant for the Russian president in March 2023 over unlawful deportations of Ukrainian children.
While the US is not a state party to the Rome Statute of the ICC and is not legally obligated under treaty law to execute ICC warrants, an in-person appearance by Putin would mark his first visit to a Western nation since the full-scale war began.
Kremlin positioning
The Kremlin has responded cautiously to public discussions regarding the Florida summit, sending mixed signals regarding whether Putin would accept an official US invitation.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov previously described speculation regarding Putin’s travel as “premature,” noting that an official determination has not yet been finalized by the presidential administration.
Peskov also dismissed prospects for a prospective bilateral encounter between Putin and President Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of the Miami meeting, reiterating Moscow’s stance that any substantive leader-level consultations could occur only in the Russian capital.

articles.title: Starlink Speeds Rise Again in Ukraine—but Key Frontline Missions Are Still Disrupted, Zelenskyy Says
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Starlink Speeds Rise Again in Ukraine—but Key Frontline Missions Are Still Disrupted, Zelenskyy Says
Starlink connectivity has improved in Ukraine following reported signals from the White House to restore higher operating speeds, but the system remains restricted, and Ukrainian forces still cannot carry out some frontline missions as before, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said during a briefing in Brussels on October 16.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s partners said there had been signals from the White House regarding the restoration of Starlink’s higher-speed capabilities.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Have they returned to the previous speed? No. But has the speed increased? Yes,” Zelenskyy said.
The restrictions have become a significant battlefield issue because Ukraine uses high-speed Starlink connectivity on rapidly moving unmanned systems. Zelenskyy stressed that Ukrainian forces do not currently use Starlink for deep strikes inside Russia.
“No, we do not use Starlink for attacks or retaliatory strikes on the territory of the Russian Federation. That is precisely why we appealed to SpaceX and the White House to open up such a capability for us. If we had it, we obviously would not be asking,” he said.
Zelenskyy described the sudden restrictions as an unpleasant and dangerous “surprise,” particularly because Starlink is used in operations intended to intercept Russia’s new jet-powered Shahed-type drones.
“We use Starlink to intercept jet-powered ‘Shaheds’ that fly in and strike our civilians, killing our families. We use special interceptors—drones that move at high speed and use Starlink,” Zelenskyy said.
He stressed that the service was not completely switched off. Instead, its effective speed limit was sharply reduced, which prevented some Ukrainian interceptor drones from keeping their satellite connection while pursuing fast-moving Russian targets.
“And when the speed was reduced, we were unable to shoot down a certain number of these ‘Shaheds.’ That is very painful and unpleasant. In other words, we were unable to provide protection for the population. The ‘Shaheds’ were flying at more than 400 kilometers per hour, while our speed was reduced to 78 km/h,” he said.
That means Russian jet-powered drones were traveling at more than 249 mph, while Ukrainian Starlink-equipped systems reportedly faced connectivity restrictions at around 48 mph.
The restrictions have also affected Ukrainian middle-strike operations against Russian military targets in occupied Ukrainian territory. Zelenskyy said Starlink connectivity had previously supported those missions, but the new limits made some of them impossible.
“And we can no longer do this,” he said.
Beyond combat missions, Zelenskyy emphasized that the restrictions have also complicated battlefield logistics. Ukrainian units use drones connected through Starlink to deliver food and water to troops holding isolated or difficult positions.
“Many people are within reach of enemy drones; we use UAVs to deliver water and food to people who have been holding positions for a long time. We use drones and Starlink. So this affected our ability to protect the population,” Zelenskyy said.
Previously, Germany called for speed restrictions affecting Starlink service in Ukraine to be lifted, stressing that Berlin itself finances part of the satellite communications equipment used by the country.

articles.title: 'Shelter in place' warning as Australians told not to travel to Middle East hub
articles.body:
In brief
- An "unpredictable" security situation means Australians shouldn't travel to Saudi Arabia, Smartraveller has warned.
- The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade website also said travel advice could change at short notice.
Australians have been warned to postpone any planned travel to Saudi Arabia after the government increased its travel advice amid a "volatile" security situation in the Middle East hub.
The Australian government updated its travel advice for Saudi Arabia and its international airport in Riyadh to "do not travel", after fighting between Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement and a Saudi-led military coalition saw strikes on the airport that killed at least 14 and wounded hundreds last week.
A strike on King Khalid International Airport on Saturday killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300, with the Houthis claiming responsibility for the deadliest attack in the kingdom in more than a decade.
The following Monday, another strike killed one person and injured 11 others, Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said, as the Houthis said the group had attacked other airports and said the worst was yet to come.
The latest advice on the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade's Smartraveller website said Australians should postpone any planned travel to Saudi Arabia, including for religious purposes, avoid travelling to King Khalid International Airport, and exercise extreme caution travelling to any other airports, amid an "unpredictable" security situation.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Following Houthi threats to target Saudi airports and airspace, "air travel is significantly disrupted at all major airports, with regular airspace closures, flight cancellations and delays", the missive read.
The government warned that "do not travel" also meant "do not transit".
"If you choose to travel despite our advice, ensure you understand the risks," it said.
What to do if you're in Saudi Arabia
The government warned that Australians in Saudi Arabia who wish to leave should do so "while commercial options remain available", and, if it is safe to do so, to consider private car, train or bus options, including to aviation hubs Abu Dhabi, in the UAE and Doha, in Qatar.
Travel warnings for Qatar and the UAE, whose transit hubs see millions of people each year, are currently at Level 2 — "exercise a high degree of caution", due to the threat of terrorism and the unpredictable security situation in the region.
Australians are advised not to travel from any Saudi airports, but if they do choose to do so, they should monitor updates, follow the advice of local authorities and airport staff, and minimise time there.
As flights were postponed or delayed with little to no notice, Smartraveller said: "do not leave for any airport until you have reconfirmed your flight with your airline".
"Military strikes and reprisal attacks have occurred across parts of the Middle East region and tensions remain elevated ... Security conditions can deteriorate quickly, and travel advice levels may change at short notice," it said.
People who choose to remain in Saudi Arabia should be prepared to shelter in place at short notice and ensure they have sufficient food, water and other essential supplies, the government warned.
"If a strike occurs, seek shelter in a substantial building and stay away from windows. Falling debris from intercepted missiles and drones also poses a risk," it said.
On Saturday, Britain's foreign office also issued a warning advising against all but essential travel to Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: All the president’s women: a familiar downward trajectory in Trump’s cabinet
articles.body:
Donald Trump is not, by any measure, a feminist. He has said so himself. But the president has often pointed to his hiring and promoting of women in an attempt to stave off criticism of both his policies and personal conduct over the years.
During his second term, however, there is one common characteristic among most of those who have departed the Trump administration.
In the space of just a few months, half of his eight female cabinet officials have either resigned or been fired. All have been replaced by men. Several other women in his administration have also departed, whether voluntarily or involuntarily.
On Friday, Trump was forced to deny reports that he was considering replacing Susie Wiles, his White House chief of staff, and the first woman to do the job. “She’s gonna be here for a long time,” he claimed.
Numerous top male officials, meanwhile, from Trump’s defense secretary Pete Hegseth, who has on multiple occasions courted global condemnation, to the widely ridiculed FBI director Kash Patel, have survived intense scrutiny and repeated calls for their resignation – and yet remain in post.
Katie Zacharia
The latest female casualty was White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, who was fired on Friday just five days into the role. After a rocky start to her tenure, sparked by a widely panned first White House press briefing on Tuesday, she had also faced questions over her legal credentials after admitting she did not pass the bar exam. The ensuing semantics battle over whether or not she is a lawyer, or an attorney, placed her in a pickle – even with the rightwing cable network Fox News.
Zacharia had taken over from Karoline Leavitt, who said in August that she had chosen to resign from the role after 20 months so she could spend more time with her young family.
Kristi Noem
In terms of firings, the first domino to fall was former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem, who was the face of Trump’s mass deportation campaign until she was unceremoniously sacked on 5 March. Her tenure was plagued by controversy, in large part amid national uproar over federal immigration enforcement operations that killed two US citizens in Minneapolis (one of whom Noem called a “domestic terrorist”, with no evidence), and coincided with a sharp decline in national support for Trump’s immigration agenda.
Her suggestion at a congressional hearing in March that Trump had known about her decision to approve a contract for a $220m ad campaign to encourage immigrants to “self-deport” – which prominently featured Noem on horseback – reportedly left Trump “pissed” and appeared to be the straw that broke the camel’s back. There had also been scrutiny of general leadership failures under Noem, as well as questions the influence of her adviser, Corey Lewandowski, who also left his role when she was ousted.
Noem was repurposed as special envoy to the so-called “Shield of the Americas” coalition and, after that arrangement expired last month, is now serving in a vaguely defined advisory role. She was succeeded as DHS secretary by Markwayne Mullin.
Pam Bondi
Next fell former attorney general and Trump loyalist Pam Bondi, who was pushed out in April after a turbulent 14 months that saw the president increasingly frustrated over her mishandling of the Department of Justice’s long-awaited release of the Epstein files. The Epstein issue became a huge political liability for Trump and infuriated his Maga base, and he also felt that Bondi had failed to sufficiently prosecute his political enemies.
Bondi revealed a month after she was ousted that she had been diagnosed with thyroid cancer. Her deputy, Todd Blanche, assumed the role in August.
It’s worth noting that commerce secretary Howard Lutnick faced public scrutiny after details emerged surrounding his past ties to Jeffrey Epstein and visits to his private island emerged. By contrast, the White House supported him after Democrats called for his resignation.
Lori Chavez-DeRemer
Also in April, former labor secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer stepped down after a Department of Labor inspector general investigation led to a series of allegations of misconduct, including having an affair with a subordinate and drinking alcohol on the job. She was replaced by Keith Sonderling.
Kash Patel has also been alleged to have been intoxicated or absent on the job. He has denied these allegations, and remains FBI director.
Tulsi Gabbard
A month later, in May, Tulsi Gabbard resigned from her position as Trump’s national intelligence director.
While she officially cited her husband’s rare cancer diagnosis, Gabbard was reportedly forced out after a tumultuous stint in which she was largely sidelined as Trump launched attacks on Venezuela and Iran. She had previously testified to Congress that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon.
Gabbard was replaced on an acting basis by Bill Pulte, a Trump loyalist with no previous experience in the intelligence sphere, and eventually by Jay Clayton.
Kimberly Guilfoyle
Earlier this week, the Trump administration asked longtime Trump ally Kimberly Guilfoyle to step down from her position as US ambassador to Greece after weeks of reports that she sought payment from a Trump donor in exchange for access to administration officials.
The only senior male official to have been somewhat punished by Trump since his return to office is Mike Waltz. The then-national security adviser was fired in May last year after inadvertently adding a journalist to a Signal group chat in which Hegseth disclosed secret war plans.
Waltz had been on thin ice with Trump for a while, and the president was reportedly annoyed by Waltz’s hawkish stance on Iran. Signalgate merely sealed his fate.
But he didn’t disappear to some obscure advisory role; Waltz was nominated to the position of US ambassador to the United Nations. Hegseth, meanwhile, was allowed to ride out the controversy and – several controversies later, including allegations of war crimes – remains in post.
Democrats have highlighted the double standard that Trump only seems to fire women in his administration – even those who are ultra-loyal to him, and decidedly less incompetent than some of their male colleagues.
“If you’re a man in the Trump administration, it seems that they reward misconduct,” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the Democratic congresswoman, observed in April.
“I wouldn’t say I’m a feminist,” Trump said in a 2018 interview. “I mean, I think that would be, maybe, going too far. I’m for women. I’m for men. I’m for everyone.”
But not everyone gets to stick around.

Ukraine Develops Full-Body Protective Armor That NATO Armies Do Not Currently Field
Ukraine is introducing a new layer of body protection for frontline troops, centrally procuring 4,700 fragmentation-resistant suits for the first time, according to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense on October 15.
The roughly two-kilogram protective system consists of a specialized jacket, trousers, and pteruges designed to shield the pelvis and upper thighs.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The pteruges include an adjustable belt and seven sections containing soft ballistic inserts: two frontal, four lateral, and one rear.
Unlike rigid armor plates, the soft ballistic packages are designed to conform to the soldier’s body while providing protection against fragments and bullets. The sections can be repositioned for fit, while the rear section includes additional padding for troops operating while seated. The suit can also be worn with a standard body armor vest, extending protection to areas that are normally left exposed.
“Our task at the Ministry of Defense is to listen to the needs of the troops and supply exactly what our warriors really need,” Deputy Defense Minister Mstyslav Banik stated. The design underwent military testing among personnel whose combat duties require high mobility before the final model was approved.
The armor is intended primarily for assault troops, medics, and other personnel operating near the line of contact, where artillery shells and drones create persistent fragmentation threats. The Ministry noted that comparable protective suits are not currently fielded by NATO countries and that a prototype of the Ukrainian design was provided to Western partners for evaluation.
Ukraine's pace of battlefield adaptation has drawn growing attention from its Western partners. Earlier in October, former US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll called it “humiliating” to watch Ukraine field better weapons despite a far smaller budget.
He argued that the US procurement system was too slow to keep pace. In May 2025, Driscoll created the 600-soldier Unmanned Assault Battalion, an experimental drones-first unit in Italy that worked alongside Ukrainian advisers.

articles.title: Midterms 2026: What Comes Next for the US and Europe?
articles.body:
The US will elect a new House of Representatives and a third of the members of the Senate in its midterm elections on 3 November. For US President Donald Trump a lot is at stake: if the Republicans lose their majority in Congress it will be far more difficult for him to pursue his policies. Europe’s press discusses the ramifications of the midterms for the US, Ukraine and Europe.
More stringent domestic controls on the way
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
El País (Spain) predicts there will be a change of course after 3 November:
“History shows that voters often punish the president’s party in mid-term elections. … This year, the Democrats are considered clear favourites to win the House of Representatives while the race for the Senate is too close to call. ... Government oversight and accountability will then be far more frequent and stringent, and foreign policy decisions will become more complex. ... Congress established the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency by law and it is the only body that can attach conditions to its budget or hold officials to account in the event of abuse. ... On 3 November, Americans will decide a large part of Washington’s political agenda.”
The tale of the stolen election
Trump could attempt to undermine the legitimacy of the election result, US expert Lauric Henneton writes in Le Monde (France):
“While Trump may fail to overturn the election result, he could succeed in reviving the narrative of a stolen election. A narrative fuelled by images, social media, investigations, legal challenges, refused election certifications and judges – who are inevitably perceived as politically biased. ... Trump is unlikely to be able to ‘steal’ the midterm elections. He could, however, attempt to convince millions of Americans that they were stolen from him, delegitimise the Democratic majority for two years, further erode electoral legitimacy, and turn 2028 into an election of revenge.”
Meeks Introduces Bill to Block Trump-Putin Diesel Deal
EU weathering the storm
Radio Kommersant FM (Russia) suspects Europe is pursuing the following strategy:
“One gets the impression that both Kyiv and the leaders of the key EU countries have, in effect, interfered in the US election campaign and, with their stance on Trump, are highlighting the failure of his policies towards Europe with the goal of bringing about a victory for the Democrats. It seems they are simply hoping to weather out the storm with this unpredictable politician who is inclined to make compromises with Moscow and wait until November 2028 in the hope that a Democratic candidate will win the next presidential election and the halcyon days of Joe Biden will return, when the US, Europe and Ukraine stood united against the Kremlin.”
Making voters believe Zelensky is the obstacle
Trump is targeting his own voter base with this announcement of a partial ceasefire, opposition news website Vot Tak (Russia) believes:
“This ‘energy truce’ conveys the impression that the situation is under control, while the allegations against Zelensky will serve as an excuse should the measures fail to produce the desired result. Trump does not need to convince everyone that Ukraine is the cause of the crisis, his aim is more modest and easier to achieve – he wants to give a sufficient number of disgruntled Republican voters a reason to believe that he is trying to resolve the situation but that someone is standing in his way.”
Even more chaos after November 3?
A Republican defeat could lead to major upheavals in foreign policy, former World Bank economist István Dobozi explains in Népszabadság (Hungary):
“If he suffers a crushing defeat, Trump might conclude that in the remaining time of his presidency he should no longer focus on minimising the short-term domestic costs, but rather on maximising his legacy in global politics. After 3 November, the US and the world could well wake up to a Trump who is politically weakened in the US and more unpredictable than ever, and whose foreign policy is focused on boosting his historical self-image. This could be particularly dangerous in the case of Iran.”
